title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: A small addition of capacity to the Kinesis Data Streams front-end fleet in US-EAST-1 pushed every server past an operating-system maximum thread-count limit. Because each front-end server creates OS threads for every other server in the fleet, the added hosts made the per-server thread count breach the OS ceiling; cache construction failed and servers were left with useless shard-maps, unable to route requests. Kinesis errored and slowed, and because many AWS services depend on Kinesis, CloudWatch, Cognito, Lambda, EventBridge and customer workloads cascaded down. Recovery was throttled by slow membership propagation and restart contention, so full Kinesis restoration took roughly 17 hours.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: The trigger — explicitly labeled by AWS as the trigger and NOT the root cause — was a small capacity addition to the Amazon Kinesis Data Streams front-end fleet in US-EAST-1, which 'began to be added to the service at 2:44 AM PST, finishing at 3:47 AM PST.' The front-end's role is narrow but foundational: 'It handles authentication, throttling, and request-routing to the correct stream-shards on the back-end clusters.' The actual root cause was an architectural coupling in the front-end's peer-coordination design: 'each front-end server creates operating system threads for each of the other servers in the front-end fleet,' so 'the total threads each server must maintain is directly proportional to the number of servers in the fleet' — thread consumption scales with fleet size N, not with traffic. Adding servers therefore raised the per-server thread count on every existing server as well as the new ones. Once the enlarged fleet was fully in service, 'the new capacity had caused all of the servers in the fleet to exceed the maximum number of threads allowed by an operating system configuration.' Crossing that OS-configured per-process ceiling did not cleanly crash the servers; it broke their routing state: 'As this limit was being exceeded, cache construction was failing to complete and front-end servers were ending up with useless shard-maps that left them unable to route requests to back-end clusters.' Because every server crossed the same shared limit at nearly the same time, and because the front-end (unlike the already-cellularized back-end) was not yet cellularized, the failure hit the whole fleet at once. First alarms fired at 5:15 AM PST; AWS narrowed the cause and determined a full front-end restart was required at 7:51 AM PST, confirmed root cause at 9:39 AM PST, took first traffic on recovered servers at 10:07 AM PST, and fully restored Kinesis at 10:23 PM PST. Recovery was slow because the same coordination design throttled it: 'It takes up to an hour for any existing front-end fleet member to learn of new participants,' and 'bringing front-end servers back online too quickly would create contention... [so] we could only add servers at the rate of a few hundred per hour.' Numerous AWS services that depend on Kinesis for telemetry and eventing — Cognito, CloudWatch, Lambda, and ECS/EKS (via EventBridge) — were degraded as a downstream cascade.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: The Kinesis Data Streams front-end is a thin routing/authentication tier: 'It handles authentication, throttling, and request-routing to the correct stream-shards on the back-end clusters.' To route requests it maintains a shard-map cache. Critically, front-end servers must stay coordinated about fleet membership, and the implementation does this per-peer: 'each front-end server creates operating system threads for each of the other servers in the front-end fleet.' This makes per-server thread usage O(N) in fleet size N — 'the total threads each server must maintain is directly proportional to the number of servers in the fleet' — and independent of request volume. As long as N stayed low enough that O(N) coordination threads (plus the server's other threads) fit under the OS-configured per-process ceiling, the fleet was stable. The November 25 capacity addition (2:44 AM to 3:47 AM PST), which AWS calls the 'trigger, though not root cause,' increased N. Because the thread cost is borne by every server, not just the new ones, the addition raised thread counts fleet-wide at once, and 'the new capacity had caused all of the servers in the fleet to exceed the maximum number of threads allowed by an operating system configuration.' The failure mode was not a clean crash: when a server could not create the threads it needed, its shard-map build did not finish — 'cache construction was failing to complete and front-end servers were ending up with useless shard-maps that left them unable to route requests to back-end clusters.' Because every server crossed the threshold at nearly the same time, the fleet degraded coherently rather than partially, which is why customer errors were broad once alarms fired at 5:15 AM PST. Recovery was constrained by the same coordination design that caused the fault: 'It takes up to an hour for any existing front-end fleet member to learn of new participants,' and 'bringing front-end servers back online too quickly would create contention between these two needs and result in very few resources being available to handle incoming requests,' so servers could be re-added only 'at the rate of a few hundred per hour.' This is why, despite root-cause confirmation at 9:39 AM PST and first servers taking traffic at 10:07 AM PST, full restoration took until 10:23 PM PST. AWS's stated remediations attack the mechanism from three angles: 'moving to larger CPU and memory servers, reducing the total number of servers and, hence, threads required by each server to communicate across the fleet' (smaller N); 'finish testing an increase in thread count limits in our operating system configuration' (more headroom under the ceiling); and 'accelerate the cellularization of the front-end fleet to match what we've done with the back-end' (bounding N per cell and containing blast radius).

text: 2020-11-25 10:31 PM PST [Restored] CloudWatch metrics and alarms fully recovered.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Architectural coupling of thread count to fleet size: each front-end server spawns one OS thread per other server in the fleet ('each front-end server creates operating system threads for each of the other servers in the front-end fleet'), so per-server thread consumption grows O(N) with fleet size rather than with load. Scaling the fleet up — normally a capacity/safety action — was itself the destabilizing force that pushed every server past the OS thread limit.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: A hard OS-level maximum-threads-per-process configuration with insufficient headroom: 'the new capacity had caused all of the servers in the fleet to exceed the maximum number of threads allowed by an operating system configuration.' A modest capacity addition was enough to exceed it fleet-wide, and AWS's remediation to 'finish testing an increase in thread count limits' indicates the limit had not been raised ahead of fleet growth.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Absence of cellularization on the front-end fleet (unlike the back-end, which AWS had already cellularized — 'accelerate the cellularization of the front-end fleet to match what we've done with the back-end'): there was no bulkhead to isolate the failure, so every front-end server hit the same shared OS limit simultaneously and failed together, giving the fault region-wide front-end blast radius.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Fragile recovery dynamics baked into the same coordination design: 'It takes up to an hour for any existing front-end fleet member to learn of new participants,' and 'bringing front-end servers back online too quickly would create contention... [so] we could only add servers at the rate of a few hundred per hour,' turning restoration into a multi-hour process (first traffic 10:07 AM PST, full recovery 10:23 PM PST).

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Wide blast radius via service dependencies on Kinesis for telemetry and eventing — 'Amazon Cognito uses Kinesis Data Streams to collect and analyze API access patterns,' 'CloudWatch uses Kinesis Data Streams for the processing of metric and log data,' 'Lambda function invocations currently require publishing metric data to CloudWatch as part of invocation,' and 'Elastic Container Service (ECS) and Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) both make use of EventBridge to drive internal workflows' — so a single-fleet fault cascaded into broad multi-service impairment.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Delayed diagnosis: first alarms at 5:15 AM PST, but the team did not narrow to a couple of candidate causes and determine that a full front-end restart was required until 7:51 AM PST, and did not confirm root cause until 9:39 AM PST, extending time-to-mitigate.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Modify Cognito webservers so they can sustain Kinesis API errors without exhausting buffers, decoupling Cognito availability from the Kinesis data plane. (AWS Cognito team · Completed as a post-incident remediation ('we have modified...'); a separate short-term Cognito mitigation was deployed at 10:15 AM PST during the event.)

text: Change support training so support engineers are regularly trained on the backup status-communication tool (the primary Service Health Dashboard depended on the impaired Cognito). (AWS Support · Completed (process change))

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Resource limits that scale with fleet size are latent scaling traps: a thread-per-peer model makes per-host thread usage grow with the whole fleet, so an ordinary, small capacity add can silently push every host over an OS ceiling at once.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Alarm on the failing resource, not just its symptoms: with no thread-consumption alarming, the first signal was downstream put/get errors ~1.5 hours after the breach — precious lead time lost to indirect detection.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Blast radius follows dependencies: a single data-plane service (Kinesis) coupled to CloudWatch, Cognito, Lambda and EventBridge turned one fleet's failure into a multi-service regional outage.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Design dependents to degrade, not die: latent buffering assumptions (Cognito exhausting buffers on upstream errors; CloudWatch metric buffers growing into memory contention that reached Lambda) converted a Kinesis fault into independent secondary failures.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Recovery must be planned as carefully as failure: slow membership propagation (up to 1h) and restart contention capped restart at a few hundred servers/hour, so the fix itself took ~12 hours — cold-start speed is a first-class reliability property.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Status-communication tooling must not share the failure domain it reports on: the primary dashboard depended on the impaired Cognito, so operators needed a rehearsed, independent backup channel.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Bound the fault domain via cellularization of the front-end fleet so thread growth (and any similar resource pressure) is contained within a cell rather than the entire fleet.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Reduce per-host peer-thread pressure by consolidating onto larger CPU/memory servers and raising the tested OS thread-count limit, giving headroom against fleet-size-driven thread growth.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Add fine-grained thread-consumption alarming to detect the actual limiting resource before it manifests as downstream request errors.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Isolate high-fan-in tenants by moving large services like CloudWatch to a separate, partitioned front-end fleet and moving the front-end cache to a dedicated fleet.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Harden dependents against upstream failure: Cognito webservers now tolerate Kinesis errors without exhausting buffers, and CloudWatch persists 3 hours of metrics locally so alarms survive a Kinesis outage.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Make recovery faster and safer by radically improving cold-start time so a throttled, contention-limited restart no longer dominates the outage duration.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Decouple operational status communications from the services being reported on, and keep support engineers regularly trained on the independent backup tool.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Failure mechanism: a fleet-size-coupled resource limit: The front-end fleet used a design in which every server maintains OS threads for every other server in the fleet, so the per-server thread count is a function of fleet size. Adding even a small amount of capacity therefore raised the thread count on all existing hosts simultaneously. When that count crossed the operating-system's configured maximum thread ceiling, the servers could no longer complete construction of their shard-map cache. The result was not a clean crash but a corrupt operating state: front-end servers came up holding useless shard-maps and could not route requests, so the whole fleet degraded in unison rather than losing a subset of hosts.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Why it cascaded across AWS: Kinesis Data Streams sits beneath a wide set of AWS control- and data-plane services, so its degradation propagated by dependency. CloudWatch buffered metric data it could not flush, and that buffering grew until it caused memory contention on downstream hosts — which in turn raised AWS Lambda function-invocation error rates. Cognito User Pools suffered elevated API failures and latency because a latent buffering bug meant its webservers could not survive sustained Kinesis errors, exhausting buffers and blocking authentication and credential access. EventBridge / CloudWatch Events processing was delayed, which in turn slowed dependent Amazon ECS/EKS provisioning and scaling and AWS Auto Scaling policies. One fleet's internal limit thus became a regional, multi-service event.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Recovery: why it took ~17 hours: Restoration could not be rushed. AWS first had to carefully reduce thread counts and remove the added capacity, then bring servers back gradually. Two properties throttled this: it takes up to an hour for any existing fleet member to learn of new participants, and restarting too quickly creates contention between membership propagation and handling incoming requests, starving request-handling and re-inducing errors. Consequently AWS could only add servers at a few hundred per hour. Restart began at 10:07 AM PST but Kinesis did not fully normalize until 10:23 PM PST — roughly 12 hours later. Dependent services recovered on their own tracks: Cognito normal by 2:18 PM, EventBridge largely resolved by 4:15 PM, CloudWatch fully recovered by 10:31 PM PST.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Organizational and systemic factors: Several systemic gaps amplified the event. There was no fine-grained alarm on thread consumption, so the first indication was indirect (put/get errors) about 1.5 hours after the breach. The front-end fleet had not yet been cellularized the way the back-end had, so there was no bulkhead to contain the thread growth to a subset. Downstream services embedded fragile assumptions (Cognito buffer exhaustion; CloudWatch unbounded metric buffering) that turned an upstream fault into independent secondary failures. And operational communication was itself in the blast radius: the primary Service Health Dashboard depended on the impaired Cognito, and support engineers were not routinely trained on the backup tool.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Cross-incident pattern: This event exemplifies a recurring class of large-scale outages: a routine, low-risk operational change (a small capacity add) interacts with a resource limit that scales with system size, and the fault then propagates along a hidden dependency web from a foundational service outward. The remediations — cellularization to bound fault domains, alarming on the true limiting resource, hardening dependents to degrade rather than fail, isolating high-fan-in tenants, and decoupling status tooling from the services it monitors — are the same structural defenses that recur across major cloud incidents. Notably, no dollar cost or affected-user count was published for this specific event, and the widely cited ~$34M Parametrix figure pertains to the separate December 7, 2021 US-EAST-1 outage, not this one.

title: AWS Kinesis OS Thread-Limit Cascade — US-EAST-1 (Nov 25, 2020)
text: Front-end restart rate ceiling: A few hundred servers per hour (limited by contention)

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: An authorized S3 engineer running an established capacity-removal playbook mistyped one input; the command removed far more servers than intended, taking down the S3 index and placement subsystems in US-EAST-1. Because a very large number of services (and AWS's own status dashboard) depend on S3, the ~4.5-hour disruption cascaded across a large fraction of the internet.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text:
Trigger. On 2017-02-28 at 9:37 AM PST, an authorized Amazon S3 team member, working from an established operational playbook, executed a command intended to remove a small number of servers from an S3 subsystem used by the S3 billing process. One of the inputs to that command was entered incorrectly, and as a result a far larger set of servers was removed than intended. This single mistyped input during a routine maintenance action was the proximate ignition of the disruption in the US-EAST-1 (Northern Virginia) Region.

Mechanism. The servers that were inadvertently removed did not belong solely to the billing subsystem; they also supported two other, far more critical S3 subsystems. The first was the index subsystem, which manages the metadata and location information of all S3 objects in the region and is necessary to serve all GET, LIST, PUT, and DELETE requests. The second was the placement subsystem, which manages allocation of new storage during PUT requests and itself requires the index subsystem to be functioning properly to operate correctly. Removing a significant portion of the capacity supporting these subsystems caused each of them to require a full restart, and while they were restarting S3 was unable to service requests. The failure therefore propagated from a peripheral billing-maintenance task into the region-wide object-storage data path.

Why safeguards and redundancy did not prevent a prolonged outage. This was not a data-loss or durability event; it was a capacity-loss and cold-start problem. Because so much capacity was removed at once, the subsystems required a complete restart rather than graceful degradation. Recovery was slow for a structural reason: AWS had not completely restarted the index subsystem or the placement subsystem in its larger regions for many years, and S3 had experienced massive growth over that period, so restarting these services and running the necessary safety checks to validate the integrity of the metadata took longer than expected.

Escalation and blast radius. The outage extended beyond S3. Other US-EAST-1 services that rely on S3 for storage were impaired while the S3 APIs were unavailable, including the S3 console, EC2 new-instance launches, EBS volumes (when data was needed from an S3 snapshot), and AWS Lambda. A compounding communication failure worsened visibility: from the beginning of the event until 11:37 AM PST, AWS could not update individual service status on the Service Health Dashboard because the SHD administration console itself had a dependency on S3 in the affected region. Recovery then proceeded in dependency order: by 12:26 PM PST the index subsystem had activated enough capacity to begin servicing GET, LIST, and DELETE requests; it was fully recovered by 1:18 PM PST; and the placement subsystem, which could only recover once the index subsystem was functional, finished recovery at 1:54 PM PST, at which point S3 was operating normally.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text:
At an engineering level the failure was a capacity-loss-induced cold restart of stateful metadata subsystems, not a corruption or durability failure. S3 in a region is decomposed into subsystems; the index subsystem is the authoritative store of object metadata and location and sits on the critical path of every GET, LIST, PUT, and DELETE request, while the placement subsystem allocates storage for new objects on PUTs and requires the index subsystem to be functioning properly. The mistyped command input removed a set of servers spanning the billing subsystem plus these two subsystems. Because the removal took capacity below what the running subsystems could tolerate, they could not simply shed the lost nodes and continue; each required a full restart, and during that restart interval S3 was unable to service requests.

The dominant factor in recovery time was the restart of the index subsystem. Restarting it required not just re-provisioning capacity but running safety checks to validate the integrity of the object metadata across the region before it could resume serving traffic. Because S3 had grown massively since the index and placement subsystems had last been fully restarted in the large regions (many years prior), the actual restart-and-validate time far exceeded expectations. The placement subsystem could not begin meaningful recovery until the index subsystem was functional, so the two recoveries were necessarily serialized: the index subsystem reached partial service (GET, LIST, DELETE) at 12:26 PM PST and full recovery at 1:18 PM PST, after which the placement subsystem (PUT path) finished recovery at 1:54 PM PST.

The corrective engineering direction confirms the mechanism. AWS was already partitioning the index subsystem into smaller units it calls 'cells' — which reduces the blast radius and per-unit restart time of any single failure — and reprioritized that work to begin immediately. It also hardened the operational tool to remove capacity more slowly and to refuse removals that would drop any subsystem below its minimum required capacity level, and it changed the Service Health Dashboard administration console to run across multiple AWS regions so status reporting no longer shares fate with the region it reports on.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: 2017-02-28 09:37 PST [Trigger] Authorized S3 team member executes an established playbook command to remove a small number of billing-subsystem servers; one input is entered incorrectly, removing a larger server set than intended.

text: 2017-02-28 ~09:37 PST [Escalation] The removed capacity crosses a threshold that forces a FULL restart of two core S3 subsystems: the index subsystem (metadata/location of every US-EAST-1 object, on the read path) and the placement subsystem (allocates storage for new objects, on the write path).

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: 2017-02-28 14:12 PST [Restored] S3 PUT/DELETE/POST (write) operations fully recovered — 4h35m after onset; region operating normally.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Insufficient tooling guardrails: the capacity-removal tool accepted an operator input that removed a much larger set of servers than intended and had no safeguard to block removals that would take a subsystem below its minimum required capacity. AWS's committed fix was to modify the tool to remove capacity more slowly and to add safeguards preventing removals below a subsystem's minimum required capacity level.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Hidden/shared infrastructure coupling: servers being removed for the peripheral billing subsystem also underpinned the critical index and placement subsystems, so a low-risk maintenance action had a high-blast-radius effect. The placement subsystem's hard dependency on the index subsystem further serialized and lengthened recovery.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Untested cold-start at scale: the index and placement subsystems had not been completely restarted in the larger regions for many years while S3 grew massively, so the restart plus metadata-integrity safety checks took far longer than expected. AWS reprioritized work to further partition the index subsystem into smaller 'cells' to reduce blast radius and restart time.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Monitoring/communication single point of failure: the Service Health Dashboard administration console depended on S3 in the same failed region, preventing per-service status updates until 11:37 AM PST and obscuring the incident's visibility. AWS's fix was to run the SHD administration console across multiple AWS regions.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Concentration of dependent services in one region: EC2 new-instance launches, EBS snapshot-dependent volumes, Lambda, and the S3 console all relied on US-EAST-1 S3, so a single-region S3 failure cascaded into multiple AWS services.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Partition the S3 index subsystem into smaller cells so recovery is faster and blast radius is smaller; improve restart time of index/placement subsystems. (AWS S3 · Committed)

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Change the AWS Service Health Dashboard to run across multiple regions so it can report status even when one region is impaired. (AWS · Committed)

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Routine, well-practised operational commands are still high-consequence: guard destructive/scaling actions with rate limits and hard minimum-capacity floors, not just runbooks.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Subsystems that are never restarted accumulate hidden restart risk; exercise cold-start/recovery paths deliberately so real recovery time is known.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Single-region dependency concentration converts a component fault into a systemic one; understand and reduce cross-service blast radius.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Status/observability control planes must not depend on the very system whose health they report.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Rate-limited capacity operations with enforced minimum-capacity guardrails on the S3 tooling.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Cellularization of the S3 index subsystem to shrink blast radius and speed recovery.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Multi-region AWS Service Health Dashboard so status reporting survives a regional impairment.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Broader operational-tool audit for unsafe fast-acting capacity actions.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Failure mechanism — why a capacity change became an outage: The command was a routine, authorized capacity-removal action, but the tooling had no floor on how much it could remove and no rate limit. Once removal crossed a threshold, the index and placement subsystems could not continue on the surviving fleet and had to cold-restart. The index subsystem is on the critical path of every S3 request — it resolves the physical location of each object — so its unavailability failed reads even though every byte of object data remained safely stored. The write path failed in parallel because the placement subsystem, which allocates new storage, both went down and itself depends on the index subsystem.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Why recovery took ~4.5 hours, not minutes: These subsystems had scaled to a very large footprint and had not been fully restarted for years. A cold start therefore had to load and integrity-check an enormous volume of metadata before it could safely serve traffic. The recovery time was dominated not by restarting processes but by the safety/consistency validation those processes must complete first — a latent, untested cost that only surfaced under a full restart. This is the classic 'we never exercise the recovery path, so we don't know its real duration' failure mode.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Blast radius — concentration risk: S3 US-EAST-1 is a foundational dependency: many other AWS services (EC2 launch, EBS, Lambda) and a large fraction of the public internet rely on it, often without the dependency being visible to the end operator. A fault in one storage subsystem in one region therefore propagated into a systemic, cross-service event. Critically, AWS's own Service Health Dashboard depended on S3 in the same region, so the primary status channel failed exactly when it was needed — an observability control plane must never share a failure domain with the system it observes.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Organizational / systemic factors: The proximate cause was human input error, but the incident is better read as a systems-design gap: safe, well-practised operations were allowed to take an irreversible, unbounded action with no guardrail, on subsystems whose recovery characteristics were unknown because they were never exercised. The durable fixes were structural (rate limits, minimum-capacity floors, cellularization, multi-region status) rather than 'be more careful' — the correct engineering response to human-error incidents.

title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption
text: Comparison & pattern: This sits in the same family as later large cloud events (e.g. the 2020 Kinesis thread-limit event and the 2025 DynamoDB DNS race, both also US-EAST-1 control-plane faults with wide cascades): a single-region control-plane component reaches an untested limit and takes down a shared dependency. The recurring lesson across all of them is blast-radius reduction (cells, regional isolation) and exercising recovery paths, not merely tightening runbooks.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 DynamoDB DNS Race Condition Cascades Across the Internet
text: A latent race condition in DynamoDB's automated DNS management system left two DNS Enactor processes racing in the us-east-1 region. An unusually delayed Enactor applied an old plan that overwrote a newer one, and a second Enactor's cleanup automation then deleted the plan as stale — instantly removing every IP address for the DynamoDB regional endpoint and leaving clients unable to resolve the service. Because core AWS control planes depend on DynamoDB, the fault cascaded: EC2's DropletWorkflow Manager fell into congestive collapse (insufficient-capacity launch failures), and NLB health-checks began flapping as new instances were brought into service before their network state propagated. DynamoDB DNS was manually corrected by 2:25 AM PDT, but full recovery of dependent services did not complete until 2:20 PM PDT on October 20, 2025 — roughly 14.5 hours after onset. Downdetector logged millions of reports across more than a thousand consumer and enterprise services.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 DynamoDB DNS Race Condition Cascades Across the Internet
text:
The immediate trigger of the October 20, 2025 disruption was a latent race condition in Amazon DynamoDB's automated DNS management system in the US-EAST-1 (Northern Virginia) Region. Per the AWS post-event summary, this race condition resulted in "an incorrect empty DNS record for the service's regional endpoint (dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com)," and the automation was then unable to repair that state. DynamoDB's endpoint DNS is managed by two cooperating automation components: a DNS Planner, which "monitors the health and capacity of the load balancers and periodically creates a new DNS plan," and a DNS Enactor, which applies those plans into Amazon Route53 and which is "designed to have minimal dependencies to allow for system recovery," operating "redundantly and fully independently in three different Availability Zones (AZs)."

The mechanism of failure was a timing collision between two independently operating Enactors. Per AWS, "Before it begins to apply a new plan, the DNS Enactor makes a one-time check that its plan is newer than the previously applied plan." On this occasion one Enactor experienced "unusually high delays" while retrying endpoint updates as the Planner produced newer plan generations. Meanwhile a second Enactor rapidly applied the newest plan across all endpoints and then "invoked the plan clean-up process, which identifies plans that are significantly older than the one it just applied and deletes them." The delayed first Enactor then applied "its much older plan to the regional DDB endpoint, overwriting the newer plan" — its one-time freshness check "was stale by this time due to the unusually high delays." When the clean-up process deleted that just-applied older plan, "all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed," leaving an empty DNS record.

The safeguards did not prevent the outcome. The redundancy design — three fully independent Enactors across three AZs — was intended to survive AZ or host failures, but this was not an infrastructure failure; it was a logical race between the redundant actors themselves, independently mutating shared Route53 state with coordination resting only on a one-time staleness check that could go stale under processing delay, paired with an aggressive clean-up step that deleted the very plan the delayed Enactor had just written. Worse, once the record was emptied, "the system was left in an inconsistent state that prevented subsequent plan updates from being applied by any DNS Enactors," so the automation could not self-heal and manual operator intervention was required.

Escalation was immediate and broad. Systems connecting to DynamoDB in us-east-1 via the public endpoint failed DNS resolution and could not connect. The failure cascaded into dependent services. EC2's DropletWorkflow Manager (DWFM), which maintains a lease for each managed droplet, began failing state checks: "Starting at 11:48 PM PDT on October 19, these DWFM state checks began to fail as the process depends on DynamoDB and was unable to complete." Even after DynamoDB DNS was restored, "DWFM had entered a state of congestive collapse and was unable to make forward progress in recovering droplet leases," requiring engineers to throttle incoming work (at 4:14 AM PDT) and perform selective host restarts (leases re-established by 5:28 AM). DWFM recovery then produced "a significant backlog of network state propagations" in Network Manager, delaying connectivity for newly launched EC2 instances. During that window, propagation lag caused NLB health checks to fail against otherwise healthy nodes: per AWS, "health checks would fail even though the underlying NLB node and backend targets were healthy," which "resulted in health checks alternating between failing and healthy" and "caused NLB nodes and backend targets to be removed from DNS, only to be returned to service when the next health check succeeded" — producing further customer-visible errors. Detection was fast: DynamoDB DNS was identified as the source at 12:38 AM PDT (roughly 50 minutes after the 11:48 PM onset); all DNS information was manually restored by 2:25 AM and primary DynamoDB disruption ended by 2:40 AM. The downstream EC2/Network Manager/NLB cascade extended recovery, with all EC2 APIs and new instance launches operating normally by 1:50 PM PDT (13:50).

title: AWS US-EAST-1 DynamoDB DNS Race Condition Cascades Across the Internet
text:
DynamoDB fronts its regional endpoint (dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) with load balancers whose membership and weights are published to Route53. Two automation components maintain this mapping. The DNS Planner "monitors the health and capacity of the load balancers and periodically creates a new DNS plan." The DNS Enactor consumes these plans and writes them into Route53; it is "designed to have minimal dependencies to allow for system recovery" and runs as three fully independent instances, one per Availability Zone, so no single AZ or host failure can stop DNS updates.

The correctness of this scheme relies on ordering: newer plans must win. The only ordering guard is that, per AWS, "Before it begins to apply a new plan, the DNS Enactor makes a one-time check that its plan is newer than the previously applied plan." This check is not re-validated at commit time, so it is only safe if the interval between check and write is short. On October 19-20, one Enactor suffered unusually high delays retrying endpoint updates while the Planner generated newer plan generations. A second, independent Enactor rapidly applied the newest plan across all endpoints, then invoked "the plan clean-up process, which identifies plans that are significantly older than the one it just applied and deletes them." The delayed first Enactor then finally applied "its much older plan to the regional DDB endpoint, overwriting the newer plan" — its freshness check having gone stale. The clean-up logic then deleted that just-applied older plan, and "all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed," producing an empty answer set. From that instant every client resolving the public endpoint failed to connect.

The empty-record end state was also a trap for the automation: "the system was left in an inconsistent state that prevented subsequent plan updates from being applied by any DNS Enactors," so the Planner/Enactor pipeline could not simply publish a corrected plan over the damage. Operators intervened manually; DynamoDB DNS was identified as the source at 12:38 AM PDT, all DNS information was restored by 2:25 AM, global table replicas caught up by 2:32 AM, and primary DynamoDB disruption ended by 2:40 AM.

The cascade illustrates control-plane dependency coupling. EC2's DropletWorkflow Manager (DWFM) maintains a lease for each managed droplet and must complete a periodic state check with each; per AWS, "Starting at 11:48 PM PDT on October 19, these DWFM state checks began to fail as the process depends on DynamoDB and was unable to complete," and leases timed out between 11:48 PM and 2:24 AM. After DynamoDB recovered, DWFM was in "congestive collapse" — pending lease-recovery work exceeded throughput and no forward progress occurred — so engineers throttled incoming work at 4:14 AM and selectively restarted DWFM hosts, re-establishing all leases by 5:28 AM. That recovery generated a large Network Manager backlog of network-state propagations (elevated latencies noted by 6:21 AM), delaying connectivity for newly launched instances until propagation normalized around 10:36 AM. During this window propagation lag made NLB health checks intermittently fail against healthy nodes: "health checks would fail even though the underlying NLB node and backend targets were healthy," which "resulted in health checks alternating between failing and healthy" and "caused NLB nodes and backend targets to be removed from DNS, only to be returned to service when the next health check succeeded." EC2 APIs and new instance launches were operating normally by 1:50 PM PDT (13:50).

AWS's corrective actions map onto the mechanism: it "disabled the DynamoDB DNS Planner and the DNS Enactor automation worldwide," committed to "fix the race condition scenario and add additional protections to prevent the application of incorrect DNS plans" before re-enabling, is "adding a velocity control mechanism to limit the capacity a single NLB can remove when health check failures cause AZ failover," is building an additional scale test suite to exercise the DWFM recovery workflow, and is improving throttling in EC2 data-propagation systems to rate-limit incoming work based on the size of the waiting queue.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 DynamoDB DNS Race Condition Cascades Across the Internet
text: Failure mechanism: how an empty DNS record was written: DynamoDB manages the IP addresses behind its regional endpoint through an automated pipeline of DNS Planners (which compute the desired record) and DNS Enactors (which apply plans). The design tolerated two Enactors operating at once. On the night of October 19, one Enactor was unusually delayed and applied a much older plan to the us-east-1 regional endpoint, overwriting the newer, correct plan. The second Enactor's cleanup routine then evaluated that older plan as stale — many generations behind the plan it had just applied — and deleted it. Because deletion removed the record's IP addresses, the endpoint was left with an incorrect empty DNS record. The bug was not in any single component behaving wrongly in isolation; it was the timing interleaving of a delayed apply followed by an age-based cleanup, i.e. a classic latent race condition that had never before lined up.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 DynamoDB DNS Race Condition Cascades Across the Internet
text: Why it cascaded: foundational dependency and congestive collapse: DynamoDB is a foundational dependency for AWS control planes, so an unresolvable endpoint did not stay contained. Starting at the same 11:48 PM PDT moment, EC2's DropletWorkflow Manager (DWFM) — which relies on DynamoDB for state — could no longer complete its state checks, and droplet leases began timing out. DWFM then entered congestive collapse: it could not make forward progress recovering leases, so EC2 launch requests returned insufficient-capacity errors. A second, distinct cascade hop hit Network Load Balancer: as recovery brought new EC2 instances online, the health-checking subsystem advertised them before their network state had propagated. Health checks flapped between healthy and failing, and NLB nodes and backend targets were repeatedly pulled from and returned to DNS, producing widespread connection errors. The single DNS fault thus fanned out through two independent failure modes into ECS/EKS/Fargate, Connect, STS, IAM, Redshift and 1,000+ downstream internet services.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 DynamoDB DNS Race Condition Cascades Across the Internet
text: Recovery: root fix fast, tail long: The root fault was corrected relatively quickly — engineers manually restored all DNS information for the regional endpoint by 2:25 AM PDT, roughly 2.6 hours after onset. But restoring DNS did not restore the dependent systems, which had accumulated their own backlog and instability. NLB health-check failures were detected by monitoring at 6:52 AM; network configuration propagation times did not return to normal until 10:36 AM; and AWS only began relaxing protective request throttles at 11:23 AM. The overall event did not end until 2:20 PM PDT — about 14.5 hours total. The long tail illustrates that in tightly coupled systems, mean-time-to-recovery is governed less by fixing the trigger than by draining the cascade it set off.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 DynamoDB DNS Race Condition Cascades Across the Internet
text: Organizational and systemic factors: Several systemic conditions turned a rare timing bug into a global event. The DNS automation lacked fencing to stop a stale actor from overwriting newer state, and its cleanup deleted a record on age alone without confirming it was inactive. Recovery subsystems like DWFM had no tested back-pressure to prevent congestive collapse. Readiness gating in NLB advertised targets before their network state propagated. And the concentration of critical control-plane dependencies in us-east-1 meant one region's fault propagated widely. AWS's remediation set — disabling the DNS automation worldwide pending a race fix and added plan-validation protections, a DWFM-recovery test suite, and an NLB velocity control — maps directly onto these systemic gaps rather than merely patching the immediate symptom.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 DynamoDB DNS Race Condition Cascades Across the Internet
text: Cross-incident pattern: DNS and automation-induced outages: This event fits a recurring industry pattern in which large-scale cloud outages originate not from hardware failure but from automation acting on authoritative shared state — frequently DNS or configuration systems — under a rare timing condition. The trigger is small and self-inflicted (an automated cleanup deleting a record), the blast radius is enormous because foundational services sit beneath everything else, and the visible damage is measured in downstream consumer apps (Snapchat, Reddit, Roblox, Venmo, Alexa, and more) rather than in the originating component. It reinforces the standing lesson that control-plane automation touching global state needs the same rigor — serialization, validation gates, blast-radius limits, and tested recovery — as the data plane it manages.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Internal Network Congestion Outage (December 7, 2021)
text: On December 7, 2021, an automated capacity-scaling operation on a service hosted in AWS's main network in US-EAST-1 provoked unexpected behavior from a large population of internal clients, generating a surge of connection activity that overwhelmed the networking devices bridging AWS's internal network and its main network. Rising latency and errors drove clients to retry more aggressively, creating a self-reinforcing congestion loop — effectively a self-inflicted internal denial of service. Because the internal network hosts foundational services (monitoring, internal DNS, authorization, and parts of the EC2 control plane), the congestion cascaded into control-plane, authentication, DNS, and API failures across dozens of services for roughly seven hours. The same congestion blinded AWS's own real-time monitoring, slowing diagnosis, and impaired the Service Health Dashboard tooling from failing over to its standby region, delaying public communication.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Internal Network Congestion Outage (December 7, 2021)
text:
TRIGGER (ignition). At 7:30 AM PST on December 7, 2021, an automated activity to scale capacity of one of the AWS services hosted in AWS's "main AWS network" triggered unexpected behavior from a large number of clients residing on AWS's separate "internal network." Per AWS, the internal network hosts foundational services — monitoring, internal DNS, authorization services, and parts of the EC2 control plane — while the main AWS network runs the majority of AWS services and all customer applications. The scaling action provoked those internal-network clients to generate a sudden, large surge of connection activity directed across the boundary between the two networks.

MECHANISM (propagation and congestion collapse). The connection surge overwhelmed the networking devices that bridge the internal network and the main AWS network, delaying communication between the two networks and producing elevated latency and errors for services that had to cross the boundary. The affected clients responded to this degraded service with still more connection attempts and retries, creating a self-amplifying feedback loop — a retry storm and classic congestion collapse — in which the response to congestion (retrying) directly increased the congestion, so the system could not drain on its own.

WHY REDUNDANCY / FAILOVER DID NOT ABSORB IT. AWS states the two networks are connected with multiple, geographically isolated networking devices, with capacity scaled significantly to ensure high availability. That redundancy did not rescue the system because the failure was not a device loss but an aggregate-load problem, and the load was self-sustaining: AWS's networking clients have well-tested request back-off behaviors, but "a latent issue prevented these clients from adequately backing off during this event." With back-off ineffective, retry pressure remained high on every redundant path simultaneously, so there was no healthy path to fail over to.

DETECTION AND ESCALATION. The congestion immediately impacted the availability of real-time monitoring data for AWS's internal operations teams, impairing their ability to find the source of the congestion and resolve it. Operators fell back to logs and initially identified elevated internal DNS errors; because internal DNS is foundational and this traffic was believed to be contributing to the congestion, teams focused on moving internal DNS traffic off the congested paths, which fully cleared DNS resolution errors by 9:28 AM PST. (Note: AWS frames the DNS work as a legitimate contributing-load remediation, not as a misdirected hypothesis.) Recovery then proceeded by identifying the largest traffic sources, isolating them onto dedicated networking devices, and disabling some heavy internal-network traffic sources. Congestion significantly improved by 1:34 PM PST and all network devices fully recovered by 2:22 PM PST. Dependent customer services trailed into the evening as backlogs cleared: EC2 APIs began recovering ~1:15 PM (new-instance launches lagging, ~2:40 PM), Route 53 APIs recovered 2:30 PM, STS fully recovered 4:28 PM, API Gateway largely recovered 4:37 PM, and EventBridge latency normalized 6:40 PM. Secondary operational impact: support-case creation was impacted from 7:33 AM to 2:25 PM PST, and AWS's Service Health Dashboard was impaired because its tooling depended on the affected internal network.

This root cause is the vendor account of record: AWS's own post-event summary (aws.amazon.com/message/12721) is the only published post-incident review. No regulator, court, or government body published a separate finding for this availability event, so the mechanism rests entirely on AWS's self-reported account.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Internal Network Congestion Outage (December 7, 2021)
text:
The event is a textbook congestion collapse driven by an unbounded retry feedback loop across a two-network boundary. AWS operates a customer-facing "main AWS network" (running the majority of AWS services and all customer applications) and a separate "internal network" hosting foundational services — monitoring, internal DNS, authorization, and parts of the EC2 control plane. The two are joined by multiple, geographically isolated networking devices that provide routing and network address translation, with capacity scaled for high availability. At 7:30 AM PST an automated capacity-scaling operation for a service on the main network caused a large population of internal-network clients to behave unexpectedly, opening a large surge of new connections across those bridge devices.

The bridge devices became the bottleneck. Once their capacity was exceeded, cross-network communication accrued latency and errors, and the clients interpreted this degraded service as a signal to retry. In a healthy system, exponential back-off causes offered load to decay under congestion, letting queues drain. Here a latent bug in the client back-off implementation defeated that mechanism — AWS's clients "have well tested request back-off behaviors...but a latent issue prevented these clients from adequately backing off." Offered load therefore stayed at or above device capacity, the defining condition of congestion collapse: throughput does not recover because retrying regenerates load faster than it drains.

Geographic redundancy of the bridge devices provided no relief because the failure mode was aggregate offered load, not device failure; every redundant device saw the same undamped retry flood, so there was no healthy path to fail over to. Compounding this, AWS's real-time monitoring rode the same congested internal network, so telemetry that would normally localize the hotspot was itself delayed or unavailable, pushing operators to logs. They identified elevated internal DNS errors and, believing that traffic was contributing to congestion, moved internal DNS traffic off the congested paths — a legitimate load-shedding step (not a misdiagnosis) that cleared DNS resolution errors by 9:28 AM PST.

Recovery required manually breaking the feedback loop rather than waiting for self-resolution: after the DNS reroute, operators identified the largest traffic sources, isolated them onto dedicated devices, and disabled some heavy internal-network traffic sources to reduce offered load. These steps drove offered load below capacity, letting congestion improve (1:34 PM) and devices fully recover (2:22 PM), after which dependent services drained backlogs over the following hours (EC2 APIs from ~1:15 PM, Route 53 2:30 PM, STS 4:28 PM, API Gateway 4:37 PM, EventBridge 6:40 PM). AWS's committed fixes target each link: it immediately disabled the triggering automated scaling activity (remove the ignition), committed to deploy the client back-off fix over roughly the following two weeks (restore load decay), deployed additional network configuration to protect the affected devices (bound the blast radius), and planned a new, multi-region Service Health Dashboard and support architecture (decouple status reporting from the impaired path).

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Internal Network Congestion Outage (December 7, 2021)
text: Failure mechanism: a self-inflicted internal denial of service: The event began with a routine-looking automated capacity-scaling operation, not a hardware fault or external attack. That operation provoked unexpected behavior from a large population of internal clients, which flooded the networking devices bridging AWS's internal network and its main network with connection activity. The trigger itself was momentary; what made it dangerous was the client response. As the bridging devices saturated, latency and error rates rose, and the affected clients reacted by opening still more connections and issuing more retries. That positive-feedback loop is the defining characteristic of the incident: the system attacked itself, sustaining congestion long after the initial scaling surge would otherwise have dissipated.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Internal Network Congestion Outage (December 7, 2021)
text: Why it cascaded so widely: The severity was not a function of the bridging devices alone but of what depends on the internal network. AWS runs foundational services there — monitoring, internal DNS, authorization, and parts of the EC2 control plane. Congestion on that shared substrate therefore did not stay contained to one service; it propagated into DNS resolution failures, authentication (STS) errors, control-plane API failures for EC2 and containers, and login/console impairment. Services whose control plane or client path crossed the internal network — ELB, CloudWatch, API Gateway, EventBridge, Amazon Connect, and even S3/DynamoDB access via VPC endpoints — inherited the failure, while RDS, EMR and WorkSpaces could not create resources because new EC2 launches were blocked and Redshift saw login failures via STS. Notably, AWS reported that Lambda continued to operate normally. A single congested failure domain became an ecosystem-wide event.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Internal Network Congestion Outage (December 7, 2021)
text: Recovery: constrained by blindness and caution: Two factors stretched recovery to roughly seven hours. First, the congestion degraded operators' own real-time monitoring, so the teams could not quickly pinpoint the source — they were diagnosing a network problem with the network instrument impaired. Second, because much of the main network and most customer workloads were still functioning, operators deliberately moved slowly to avoid harming healthy systems. Recovery was therefore incremental and prioritized: internal DNS was restored first (09:28), congestion eased through the early afternoon (13:34), container APIs normalized (13:35), all network devices fully recovered and the Console returned (14:22), and dependent services such as Amazon Connect trailed until 16:41 as their upstream API Gateway healed.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Internal Network Congestion Outage (December 7, 2021)
text: Organizational and systemic factors: Several systemic choices shaped the outcome. Concentrating foundational and globally-scoped control-plane services on a single internal network created a large correlated failure domain. Client retry logic lacked sufficient backpressure to prevent amplification under stress. Observability shared fate with the monitored network, defeating the very tooling meant to accelerate diagnosis. And the Service Health Dashboard tooling could not fail over to its standby region, so the public communication channel shared fate with the outage it needed to describe — compounding customer uncertainty at the worst moment.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Internal Network Congestion Outage (December 7, 2021)
text: Cross-incident pattern: This outage fits a recurring pattern in large-scale distributed systems: a small, automated, control-plane action interacts with retry/feedback dynamics and shared foundational dependencies to produce an outsized, cascading failure. The same ingredients — an automated change as trigger, a metastable congestion or retry loop that persists after the trigger, foundational services (DNS/auth/control plane) as the amplifier, and monitoring or status tooling that shares fate with the failure — recur across major cloud and internet outages. The durable defenses are likewise consistent: retry discipline with backpressure, out-of-band observability, decoupling of critical services from shared substrates, independent status/communication paths, and reduced single-region concentration.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Cooling/Thermal Event and use1-az4 Power Loss
text: On 7 May 2026 cooling systems failed in AWS's use1-az4 availability zone in US-EAST-1 (Northern Virginia). As data-hall temperatures crossed operating thresholds, servers automatically shut down to protect hardware, cutting power to the EC2 instances and EBS volumes hosted on that gear. The compute and storage loss cascaded to dependent services — IoT Core, ELB, NAT Gateway and Redshift — with elevated error rates and slower provisioning. AWS shifted traffic off the impaired zone and advised customers to relaunch or redistribute workloads in other US-EAST-1 availability zones. AWS first flagged the problem at 5:25 PM PDT on 7 May and restored cooling to pre-incident capacity at 1:50 PM PDT on 8 May, roughly 20 hours 25 minutes later. Downstream, Coinbase reported a multi-hour outage in which users could not trade or move funds. No formal AWS post-incident report was published in the available sources.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Cooling/Thermal Event and use1-az4 Power Loss
text:
On the evening of Thursday, 2026-05-07 (PDT), a cooling-system failure occurred in a single AWS data center serving the use1-az4 Availability Zone of the US-EAST-1 region (Northern Virginia). Per press coverage of AWS's own Health Dashboard, "AWS confirmed the outage was due to overheating caused by a cooling failure at its North Virginia data center, US-East-1, which is a heavily used region" (CRN). This "cooling failure" is the highest-level cause AWS disclosed; the specific reason the cooling plant failed (mechanical, controls/BMS, coolant-loop, or power-to-cooling) was never publicly explained, so the authoritative causal record stops at "cooling failure."

The mechanism that turned lost cooling into a service outage was thermal-protection automation. As temperatures climbed past design limits, "servers automatically shut down when the temperatures exceeded the operating thresholds in order to protect the hardware" (Network World). That automated shutdown is the most likely source of the "loss of power" AWS reported: "EC2 instances and EBS volumes hosted on impacted hardware are affected by the loss of power during the thermal event" in the use1-az4 Availability Zone (Network World). AWS's wording ties the power loss to the thermal event rather than to a utility, UPS, or generator fault; on that basis this incident is best read as a thermal event whose "power loss" was a protective de-energization of servers, not a primary electrical-supply failure. AWS did not, however, explicitly rule out an electrical fault, so the "protective shutdown, not electrical" reading is a well-supported interpretation, not an AWS-stated fact.

Impact then propagated along AWS's service dependency graph. AWS's first post came at 5:25 PM PDT; by 6:47 PM PDT it warned that "Other AWS services that depend on the affected EC2 instances and EBS volumes in this Availability Zone may also experience impairments" (Network World). Network World names IoT Core, ELB, NAT Gateway, and Redshift as affected; CRN additionally reports SageMaker, ElastiCache, and Amazon EKS. Recovery was protracted: at 8:06 PM PDT AWS said "progress is slower than originally anticipated," and at 10:11 PM PDT it reported only "incremental progress to restore cooling systems," with services "experiencing elevated error rates and latencies for some workflows." Power was restored to the AZ "several hours after the thermal event occurred" (CRN), but full cooling capacity was not restored to pre-incident levels until 1:50 PM PDT Friday 2026-05-08 — roughly 20 hours after the first report. Coinbase was disrupted for about seven hours (CRN).

Important caveat: no AWS official post-incident review (PIR/RFO/aws.amazon.com/message) was located. The entire causal record rests on two press summaries of Health Dashboard updates, so the disclosed cause is "cooling failure" with the underlying failure mode and the state of cooling redundancy both undisclosed.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Cooling/Thermal Event and use1-az4 Power Loss
text:
The failure chain is a thermal-loss-to-protective-shutdown sequence in a data hall. Under normal operation the use1-az4 cooling system removes heat dissipated by dense racks of EC2/EBS host hardware, holding component temperatures within a design envelope. When cooling failed on 2026-05-07, heat removal fell below heat generation and rack temperatures rose. Server firmware/BMC thermal-protection logic continuously compares inlet, CPU, and component sensors against configured operating thresholds; once those thresholds were crossed the logic triggered automatic shutdown: per AWS, "servers automatically shut down when the temperatures exceeded the operating thresholds in order to protect the hardware" (Network World). This is a deliberate hardware-preserving trade — the platform sheds its own power rather than risk sustained over-temperature damage.

Because the compute/storage substrate lost power, AWS characterized the customer-facing effect as a "loss of power during the thermal event" affecting hosted EC2 instances and EBS volumes in use1-az4 (Network World). Read against AWS's wording, this "power loss" is best interpreted as a protective de-energization of servers tied to the thermal event rather than a failure of the electrical distribution (utility, UPS, generators); AWS did not explicitly confirm or exclude an electrical fault, so this remains an interpretation rather than a disclosed fact. The blast radius then propagated along AWS's dependency graph: managed services running data or control paths on EC2/EBS in that AZ — IoT Core, ELB, NAT Gateway, and Redshift (Network World), plus SageMaker, ElastiCache, and EKS (CRN) — began "experiencing elevated error rates and latencies for some workflows" (Network World).

Recovery required restoring physical cooling capacity before shut-down hardware could be safely brought back and kept online, which is why power returned to the AZ "several hours after the thermal event" (CRN) while full cooling capacity was not restored to pre-incident levels until 1:50 PM PDT the next day (~20 hours from the first 5:25 PM PDT report, an approximate elapsed-time inference). The public technical record does not resolve the mechanism beneath the cooling failure, nor whether/why cooling redundancy failed to prevent the threshold breach — both remain undisclosed by AWS, and no official post-incident review was published.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Cooling/Thermal Event and use1-az4 Power Loss
text: Failure mechanism: The incident began as an environmental fault: cooling systems failed in use1-az4. As the data hall heated past operating thresholds, servers executed their designed thermal-protection response and powered themselves off to avoid heat damage. That autonomous shutdown is the pivot point of the whole event — it converted a cooling problem into a simultaneous, correlated power loss across the EC2 instances and EBS volumes hosted on the affected hardware. Both Network World and The Register independently describe this power-loss-during-thermal-event mechanism, giving the root cause two-source corroboration.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Cooling/Thermal Event and use1-az4 Power Loss
text: Why it cascaded: EC2 and EBS are not leaf services; they are the compute and block-storage substrate on which much of AWS is built. When they lost power, the impairment radiated outward to IoT Core, ELB, NAT Gateway and Redshift, and surfaced to customers as slower provisioning, elevated error rates and higher latencies. The cascade continued beyond AWS: Coinbase's Raft-based matching engine, Kafka streaming and order-routing services were disrupted, and — by Coinbase's own account — three of five quorum nodes were lost, enough to break consensus and halt trading. The event is therefore a textbook demonstration of how a single-hall physical fault propagates up a dependency stack into a customer-facing financial outage.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Cooling/Thermal Event and use1-az4 Power Loss
text: Recovery: Recovery was gated by the environment. AWS confirmed the use1-az4 problem at 5:25 PM PDT on 7 May, warned of cascading service impairments at 6:47 PM, reported cooling restoration progressing 'slower than anticipated' by ~8:06 PM, brought additional cooling capacity online with some racks recovering by 10:11 PM, published a fuller explanation at 6:51 AM PDT on 8 May, and restored cooling to pre-incident capacity at 1:50 PM PDT — about 20 hours 25 minutes after onset. Racks could only return once temperatures were safe again, so cooling restoration was the critical path. In parallel, AWS shifted traffic off the impaired zone and steered customers toward other US-EAST-1 zones. Coinbase's own recovery took much of the following day via a staged cancel-only, then auction, then normal re-enable sequence.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Cooling/Thermal Event and use1-az4 Power Loss
text: Organizational and systemic factors: Two structural choices shaped the impact. On the AWS side, the concentration of workload in US-EAST-1 means any hall-level fault there has amplified consequences — this is the same region behind a ~15-hour, 70-plus-service outage in October 2025. On the customer side, Coinbase's loss of a quorum majority within the affected zone, with all five Raft nodes in a single cluster placement group, indicates consensus-critical components were not spread widely enough across availability zones to survive a single-AZ loss. Coinbase's four remediation items — cross-zone recovery, better quorum restoration, multi-AZ messaging and expanded DR testing — are all aimed at that gap, though the source reports them as committed action items without owners, deadlines or verification.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Cooling/Thermal Event and use1-az4 Power Loss
text: Cross-incident pattern: The May 2026 thermal event extends a recurring 'notorious US-EAST-1' pattern. The immediately preceding major outage (19-20 October 2025) ran roughly 15 hours and cascaded across more than 70 AWS services after a DynamoDB DNS race condition; the May event is shorter in service breadth but comparable in duration and again triggered by an infrastructure fault localized to the region. The through-line is not a single repeated root cause but a repeated topology: heavy dependence on one region, foundational services with wide blast radius, and downstream customers whose own architectures assume more isolation than a correlated AZ-level failure actually provides.

title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text: On 28 September 2020 a service update meant only for an internal Azure AD validation test ring crashed on startup and, because of a latent defect in the Safe Deployment Process (SDP) tooling, was pushed straight into global production. The same defect corrupted the deployment metadata so that all deployment rings were targeted at once and the automated rollback could not run, forcing a slower manual recovery. Users were locked out of Azure Portal, Microsoft 365, Teams, Exchange/Outlook and downstream apps for roughly five hours end-to-end. It is a textbook identity-plane blast-radius event: a single canary-scoped change became a worldwide authentication failure.

title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text:
TRIGGER. Starting at approximately 21:25 UTC on 28 September 2020, Microsoft deployed a service update to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) backend service. The update was intended to reach only an internal validation test ring — an isolated slice containing no customer data, used to catch defects before broad exposure. The update contained a latent code defect that caused the Azure AD backend service to crash on startup. Per Microsoft's RCA (Tracking ID SM79-F88): "A service update targeting an internal validation test ring was deployed, causing a crash upon startup in the Azure AD backend services." Had the update been confined to the test ring, the crash would have been contained to a non-customer-facing slice.

ROOT CAUSE — FAILURE OF THE SAFE DEPLOYMENT PROCESS. The safeguard that should have limited blast radius is Microsoft's Safe Deployment Process (SDP), a ringed-rollout system that promotes changes progressively so a defective build is caught in a small ring before reaching production. The true root cause was a latent code defect in the SDP system itself, which delivered the crashing update straight to global production instead of confining it to the validation ring. In Microsoft's words: "A latent code defect in the Azure AD backend service Safe Deployment Process (SDP) system caused this to deploy directly into our production environment, bypassing our normal validation process." The crashing service update was the payload; the SDP defect was the safeguard failure that let it out globally.

NOTE ON MECHANISM DETAIL. Some reconstructions state that the SDP mis-targeted rings because it could not "interpret deployment metadata" and therefore "targeted all rings concurrently." Microsoft did not publish that level of internal detail in the canonical RCA, so it is treated here as unverified elaboration rather than an established Microsoft finding. What Microsoft stated is only that a latent SDP code defect deployed the update directly into production, bypassing validation.

PROPAGATION / BLAST RADIUS. Azure AD is the shared identity and authentication plane for the Microsoft cloud, so a global crash of its backend translated directly into authentication failures across the ecosystem. Between roughly 21:25 UTC on 28 Sep and 00:23 UTC on 29 Sep 2020, customers may have encountered errors performing authentication operations for all Microsoft and third-party applications and services that depend on Azure AD. Impact was worldwide and varied by region and time of day, but the specific per-region success-rate percentages circulated in some write-ups could not be confirmed against Microsoft's primary RCA and are not asserted here as fact.

WHY RECOVERY WAS SLOW — IMPAIRED AUTOMATED ROLLBACK. The standard mitigation for a bad rollout is automated rollback to the last known-good state. That path was impaired for the same underlying reason: the deployment metadata driving the change had been corrupted, so the automated rollback could not cleanly restore a known-good state, and engineers had to fall back to a manual mitigation that bypassed the SDP system. This coupling — the deployment path and its automated recovery path both depending on the corrupted metadata — is why the fastest remedy was unavailable and recovery was extended. Additionally, a separate Azure AD backup authentication system that could have masked authentication failures had not yet been rolled out to all key services (its expedited rollout appears as a committed corrective action).

DETECTION, MITIGATION, AND CORRECTIVE ACTIONS. Monitoring detected the unhealthy condition within about 5 minutes and engineering was engaged immediately. Because automated rollback was impaired, engineers escalated to a manual service-configuration update that bypassed the SDP system; recovery was further gated on restarting crashed backend instances and rebuilding a healthy quorum. Enough backend capacity was healthy to meet normal operational parameters by 00:23 UTC on 29 Sep, with residual impact clearing thereafter. Microsoft's committed corrective actions included fixing the SDP code defect, applying additional protections to the backend SDP system, expediting rollout of the Azure AD backup authentication system to all key services, and expanding the scope and frequency of rollback operation drills. (Specific intermediate timeline minute-markers and per-region percentages in the reconstruction were not verifiable against the primary source.)

title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text:
Microsoft operates a ringed Safe Deployment Process (SDP): changes are promoted through progressively larger rings, beginning with an internal validation test ring that contains no customer data, so a defective build is exposed in a tiny blast radius before promotion to production rings.

In this incident two faults combined. First, an Azure AD backend service update carried a code defect that caused the service process to crash on startup, preventing affected backend instances from serving authentication once they loaded it. Second, and decisively, a latent code defect in the SDP system itself caused that crashing update to reach global production instead of being confined to the validation ring. Microsoft's canonical statement is: "A latent code defect in the Azure AD backend service Safe Deployment Process (SDP) system caused this to deploy directly into our production environment, bypassing our normal validation process." The ringed gate that exists to prevent global exposure was short-circuited by a fault in the gate mechanism, not by an operator bypassing it. Deeper mechanism claims sometimes attached to this event (that the SDP could not "interpret deployment metadata" and therefore "targeted all rings concurrently") go beyond what Microsoft published and are not asserted here as established fact.

Because Azure AD is the shared token-issuing / authentication backend for the Microsoft cloud, the crash-on-startup manifested as failed authentication operations for every dependent Microsoft and third-party service. Instances that took the bad update crashed; as capacity cycled down, the pool of healthy backend instances able to serve authentication collapsed, driving authentication success rates down worldwide (severity varied by region and local peak load, though the precise per-region percentages in circulation could not be confirmed against the primary RCA).

Recovery was impaired by the same corrupted artifact. Automated rollback is designed to restore the last known-good state, but the deployment metadata had been corrupted, so the automated path could not cleanly revert the change; engineers escalated to a manual service-configuration update that bypassed the SDP system. Even after the correct configuration was applied, recovery remained gated on restarting the crashed backend instances and rebuilding a healthy quorum, which is why normal operational parameters were not met until 00:23 UTC on 29 Sep 2020, with residual impact clearing afterward. The engineering lesson embedded in the corrective actions is the coupling risk between the deployment system and its automated recovery path: a single metadata corruption both caused the outage and disabled its fastest remedy. Microsoft's committed actions were to fix the SDP defect, apply additional protections to the backend SDP system, expedite rollout of the Azure AD backup authentication system to all key services, and expand the scope and frequency of rollback operation drills.

title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text: Your safety system is part of your attack surface: a latent defect in the Safe Deployment Process — the tooling designed to prevent global blast radius — was precisely what created it. Progressive-rollout tooling must itself be validated as safety-critical.
