title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text: Failure mechanism: the safety net became the weapon: The trigger was mundane — a service update aimed at an internal validation test ring crashed on startup. In a healthy pipeline that crash is the point: the canary ring catches it and nothing ships. Here, a latent code defect in the Safe Deployment Process corrupted the system's interpretation of deployment metadata, so the ring scoping that should have confined the change instead evaluated to 'all rings.' The crash-on-startup build was therefore deployed to global production concurrently, bypassing validation entirely. The very mechanism designed to make deployments safe was the mechanism that made this one catastrophic.

title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text: Why it cascaded to a global blast radius: Azure Active Directory is the identity control plane for the entire Microsoft cloud, so the fault did not stay contained to one service. With backend instances crashing and no healthy instances to issue tokens, authentication calls returned HTTP 503, and every product that logs in through AAD failed together: Azure Portal, Microsoft 365, Teams, Exchange/Outlook, and even some Office desktop and Visual Studio installations. Impact spanned both Azure Public and Azure Government clouds. Regional authentication success rates fell sharply and unevenly — Americas as low as 17% while Europe held near 81% — reflecting how the manual, staged recovery brought regions back at different rates. Downstream third parties were plausibly caught too: The Register noted unconfirmed claims that the Azure-based RapidDeploy Nimbus emergency-dispatch platform was affected, illustrating how far an identity-plane fault can reach beyond the operator's own catalog.

title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text: Recovery: coupled failure and recovery paths: The outage ran long — roughly three hours to normal operational parameters and about five hours end-to-end — precisely because the recovery path shared a failure mode with the deployment path. Automated rollback could not execute cleanly because the same latent SDP defect had already corrupted the deployment metadata it relied on; Microsoft even posted mid-incident that it was 'not observing an increase in successful connections after rolling back.' Engineers fell back to a slower manual rollback and staged re-enablement of instances beginning around 22:47 UTC, which is why success rates recovered region by region rather than all at once. The authoritative RCA (Tracking ID SM79-F88) fixes impact start at 21:25 UTC on 28 September, return to normal parameters at 00:23 UTC, and residual instances fully cleared by 02:25 UTC on 29 September.

title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text: Organizational and systemic factors: Beyond the code, the incident exposed systemic fragilities. Identity centralization concentrates blast radius by design — convenient until the control plane fails, at which point everything fails together. The deployment tooling was trusted as a safety guarantee without an independent check that the safety system itself was behaving. Customer communication also lagged the impact, prompting a specific corrective commitment to post an initial notice within 15 minutes of impact. Contextually, this was the second major Azure disruption in roughly two weeks and came shortly after Microsoft's Ignite conference, sharpening scrutiny on the reliability of a service so many organizations depend on.

title: Azure Active Directory Global Authentication Outage (September 28, 2020)
text: Cross-incident pattern: the automation-that-globalizes-a-canary: This event is a canonical instance of a recurring cloud failure pattern: a change intended for a tiny scope is amplified to global scope by the automation meant to contain it, and then the automated remediation fails through the same defect. The countermeasures generalize across providers — validate the safety/rollout system as safety-critical software, keep the rollback path independent of any state a deployment defect can corrupt, and add an independent gate that blocks crash-on-startup builds regardless of ring targeting. Notably, a separate SharePoint/OneDrive disruption the following morning (UK time) stemmed from a change Microsoft put in place to mitigate this AAD outage — a distinct follow-on event, not the same defect — a reminder that co-occurring symptoms can have different (even causally-linked-but-separate) root causes and must be analyzed independently.

title: Azure Front Door Global Outage: Inadvertent Cross-Build Config Change Trips Latent Data-Plane Crash Bug (29 Oct 2025)
text: On 29 October 2025 an inadvertent customer configuration change to Azure Front Door (AFD) — Microsoft's global edge/CDN and traffic-routing layer — generated incompatible configuration metadata because the change sequence spanned two different control-plane build versions. That metadata exposed a latent bug in the AFD data plane, causing nodes to crash during asynchronous processing as the bad config propagated. A deployment protection safeguard activated and blocked further new changes, but it could not stop the already-propagated config: the crash surfaced asynchronously, after propagation, rather than synchronously at deploy time. Within roughly four minutes the config reached a majority of edge sites and within roughly ten minutes the crash had replicated across all edge sites globally. Recovery was complicated because the Last Known Good (LKG) snapshot had itself been updated with the corrupted config; Microsoft recovered by manually editing the latest LKG to strip the offending customer entries — deliberately declining a clean rollback — then redeploying, blocking further customer config propagation, and failing the Azure Portal away from AFD. Customer impact ran from 15:41 UTC on 29 Oct to mitigation at 00:05 UTC on 30 Oct, about 8.5 hours.

title: Azure Front Door Global Outage: Inadvertent Cross-Build Config Change Trips Latent Data-Plane Crash Bug (29 Oct 2025)
text:
The Azure Front Door (AFD) global outage of 29-30 October 2025 (Tracking ID YKYN-BWZ) originated in a control-plane/data-plane version-compatibility gap, not a single invalid change. Per Microsoft's official Post Incident Review (Azure status history, YKYN-BWZ), a sequence of individually valid customer configuration changes made across two different control-plane build versions produced "incompatible customer configuration metadata" that "exposed a latent bug in the data plane." The defect went undetected because, in Microsoft's words, "not all features are validated across different control plane build versions" - so this specific cross-build combination was never exercised by validation before reaching edge servers.

The mechanism that turned a latent bug into a global outage was the timing of processing versus validation. The pipeline processed and propagated the metadata before the defect surfaced: the data-plane crash "surfaced asynchronously, after approximately five minutes," so at validation and rollout time the configuration still appeared healthy and passed the pipeline's gates. Microsoft's status update, as reported by Build5Nines, framed the trigger to customers as "an inadvertent tenant configuration change" arising from "a faulty tenant configuration deployment process."

The safeguards that should have contained this failed for two compounding reasons. First, a genuine software defect in the deployment pipeline: "Our protection mechanisms, to validate and block any erroneous deployments, failed due to a software defect." Second, and decisively, the delayed manifestation meant the bad configuration was still treated as healthy when the staged rollout advanced - so it propagated to the majority of edge sites and the system "automatically updated the LKG [Last Known Good] snapshot with corrupted configurations." This poisoned the very rollback lever intended for fast recovery: reverting to LKG would have re-applied the failure, forcing manual editing instead.

Escalation into a platform-wide outage followed from node failure and traffic redistribution. Per the status update, "the change introduced an invalid or inconsistent configuration state that caused a significant number of AFD nodes to fail to load properly," and "as unhealthy nodes dropped out of the global pool, traffic distribution across healthy nodes became imbalanced, amplifying the impact and causing intermittent availability even for regions that were partially healthy." Users saw connection-timeout errors and DNS resolution issues across services fronted by AFD/CDN - including Azure Portal, Azure SQL Database, Microsoft 365, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and Microsoft Entra ID - over the official impact window of 15:41 UTC on 29 October to 00:05 UTC on 30 October 2025 (about 8.5 hours).

Recovery was deliberately slow because the normal fast path (LKG rollback) was unavailable. Engineers manually edited the LKG snapshot to remove the problematic configurations rather than reverting to it, blocked all new customer configuration changes (about 17:30 UTC), deployed the corrected configuration (about 17:40 UTC), and then converged carefully by rebalancing traffic gradually across edge sites to avoid re-triggering the load imbalance. This is a genuine vendor root-cause document; no independent or regulatory postmortem exists, and some secondary details circulating in third-party writeups (an alleged October 9 precursor incident, specific remediation metrics) are not confirmed by the primary sources.

title: Azure Front Door Global Outage: Inadvertent Cross-Build Config Change Trips Latent Data-Plane Crash Bug (29 Oct 2025)
text:
At an engineering level the failure chain hinges on an ordering hazard between configuration processing and configuration validation in the AFD control-plane-to-data-plane pipeline. Customer configuration changes are ingested and transformed into metadata that edge (data-plane) servers consume. During the incident, a sequence of individually valid customer changes was authored under two distinct control-plane build versions, and the resulting metadata was mutually incompatible when materialized on the data plane. Because, per Microsoft, "not all features are validated across different control plane build versions," no gate modeled this specific cross-build combination, so it was treated as valid.

The crux is that the crash "surfaced asynchronously, after approximately five minutes": the metadata was accepted, staged, and propagated while its defect was still latent. The data-plane bug was combination-specific and time-delayed, so it produced no crash signal at validation or early-rollout time. The official PIR timeline anchors impact start at 15:41 UTC; finer sub-minute steps (metadata introduced ~15:35, pre-production ~15:36, propagated ~15:39, crashes ~15:45) appear only in third-party reconstructions and should be treated as approximate.

Two safeguard layers were defeated by this timing. The validation/blocking gates were bypassed by a genuine "software defect" in the deployment pipeline ("Our protection mechanisms, to validate and block any erroneous deployments, failed due to a software defect") and by the fact that there was no crash signal to block on at validation time. The LKG rollback safeguard was defeated because propagation and the LKG-snapshot update both completed before the crash surfaced, so the LKG snapshot captured the poisoned configuration. This inverted the normal recovery model: rolling back to LKG would have re-applied the failure.

The blast radius amplified through a load-redistribution cascade characteristic of shared edge fleets. When "a significant number of AFD nodes" failed to load the configuration, they dropped out of the global pool; health-based traffic steering then imbalanced load across surviving nodes, "amplifying the impact and causing intermittent availability even for regions that were partially healthy." Because AFD fronts DNS resolution and connection termination for many first-party and customer services, this surfaced to users as connection timeouts and DNS resolution errors across Azure Portal, Azure SQL Database, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, and Entra ID.

Recovery had to route around the poisoned LKG: engineers manually edited the LKG snapshot to strip the problematic configurations rather than reverting to it, blocked all new customer configuration changes (~17:30 UTC), deployed the corrected configuration (~17:40 UTC), and then rebalanced traffic gradually across edge sites to avoid re-triggering the imbalance - reaching full resolution by 00:05 UTC on 30 October. Microsoft indicated forward-looking repairs targeting these mechanisms (moving toward synchronous per-configuration processing before production advancement, stronger pre-production/canary validation across control-plane build versions, fixing both the control-plane incompatibility and the data-plane bug, and improving recovery/isolation, consistent with Azure's published tenant-isolation resiliency direction). Specific remediation figures cited in some third-party writeups (e.g., cutting data-plane recovery from ~4.5 hours to ~1 hour, sub-10-minute recovery, ~45-minute propagation, micro-cellular sharding) are not confirmed by the primary sources reviewed and should not be stated as fact.

title: Azure Front Door Global Outage: Inadvertent Cross-Build Config Change Trips Latent Data-Plane Crash Bug (29 Oct 2025)
text: Failure mechanism: cross-version metadata meets a latent crash bug: The trigger was not a corrupt push in the conventional sense but a legitimate-looking customer configuration change whose steps happened to span two different AFD control-plane build versions. That version-straddling sequence emitted configuration metadata that was internally incompatible. When AFD nodes attempted to load and asynchronously process this metadata, it drove them into a previously latent data-plane defect that crashed the process. The bug had presumably existed dormant for some time; it required this specific, rare cross-version condition to be exercised for the first time, which is precisely why routine operation and standard validation had never surfaced it.

title: Azure Front Door Global Outage: Inadvertent Cross-Build Config Change Trips Latent Data-Plane Crash Bug (29 Oct 2025)
text: Why it cascaded globally in minutes: AFD is a single shared global edge and traffic-routing plane, and its configuration distribution is fast and broadly scoped. The incompatible config reached a majority of edge sites within about four minutes (15:39 UTC) and the resulting crash had replicated across all edge sites worldwide within about ten minutes (by ~15:45 UTC, inferred from the PIR's ~10-minute figure). There was effectively no bake time and no staging boundary to arrest the spread, so a single inadvertent change became a worldwide outage almost instantly. The deployment protection system did activate at 15:43 UTC and blocked new changes, but because the crash surfaced asynchronously after propagation rather than synchronously at deploy, the safeguard had no synchronous failure signal to block on and the already-propagated change was not stopped.

title: Azure Front Door Global Outage: Inadvertent Cross-Build Config Change Trips Latent Data-Plane Crash Bug (29 Oct 2025)
text: Recovery: edit-forward instead of roll-back: Microsoft's recovery choice is instructive. Because the latest Last Known Good configuration had itself been updated with the corrupted config, and because reverting to older versions carried its own stability risk, engineers judged that manually editing the latest LKG to strip out the offending customer configurations was the more stable path, and redeployed that. In parallel they blocked all customer config propagation at 17:30 UTC to prevent any further bad state from spreading, and failed the Azure Portal away from AFD at 17:26 UTC to restore an operator/customer access path independent of the failing layer. The corrected config reached all edge sites by 17:50 UTC, DNS recovered by 18:30 UTC, automatic traffic management resumed at 20:20 UTC, and full mitigation was declared at 00:05 UTC on 30 Oct.

title: Azure Front Door Global Outage: Inadvertent Cross-Build Config Change Trips Latent Data-Plane Crash Bug (29 Oct 2025)
text: Organizational and systemic factors: Two systemic weaknesses converted a routine change into a global incident. First, a validation coverage gap: not all features were validated across different control-plane build versions, so the incompatible-metadata condition was simply outside the test matrix. Second, an architectural coupling: config processing ran on the same instances that served traffic, and critical recovery tooling (Portal, Communications, Marketplace, support) single-depended on AFD, so the failure degraded the very systems needed to observe and recover from it. The remediation roadmap targets both classes directly — synchronous isolated config workers, backwards-compatibility testing across versions, active-active failover for critical infra, and micro-cell segmentation for tenant isolation.

title: Azure Front Door Global Outage: Inadvertent Cross-Build Config Change Trips Latent Data-Plane Crash Bug (29 Oct 2025)
text: Cross-incident pattern: shared control planes and self-inflicted global outages: This incident fits a recurring pattern in hyperscale infrastructure: the largest outages are rarely hardware or attack-driven and are instead self-inflicted configuration or control-plane faults on a shared global layer that propagate faster than any human can intervene. The distinctive lesson here is the interplay of two blind spots — a validation matrix that omitted a real production combination, and a safeguard whose detection model (synchronous) did not match the fault's behavior (asynchronous), so activating it was not enough to stop the fault. Where a change can reach the entire fleet in minutes, the only durable defenses are staged propagation with bake time, per-change synchronous validation, blast-radius segmentation, and ensuring recovery tooling never shares fate with the layer it must recover.

title: Azure South Central US: Lightning-Induced Cooling Loss and Automated Integrity Shutdown (September 2018)
text: On 4 September 2018, a high-energy thunderstorm with lightning struck southern Texas near Microsoft's South Central US datacenters. Per The Register's account of Azure's RCA, a lightning strike at 08:42 UTC switched one datacenter to generator power and overloaded surge suppressors on the mechanical cooling plant, shutting it down; the official VSTS postmortem describes voltage sags and swells on the utility feed that impacted cooling. As temperatures climbed, automated datacenter integrity procedures forced a structured power-down of servers and storage to protect hardware. Utility power was restored in roughly nine hours (per Data Center Dynamics), but recovery of services took far longer: VSTS primary recovery ran about twenty-one hours, the official VSTS incident spanned 09:45 UTC on 4 September to 00:05 UTC on 6 September (the longest outage in that service's history), and broader Azure — on the order of forty services per contemporaneous reporting — was not declared fully mitigated until 08:40 UTC on 7 September. A separate ~2-hour Release Management incident (a database going offline) occurred during recovery.

title: Azure South Central US: Lightning-Induced Cooling Loss and Automated Integrity Shutdown (September 2018)
text:
On September 4, 2018, high-energy thunderstorms struck southern Texas near Microsoft Azure's South Central US region, and multiple datacenters in the region experienced voltage sags and swells on their utility feeds. At approximately 08:42 UTC a lightning-associated electrical transient (a large voltage swell immediately followed by a large sag) hit one datacenter: it switched to generator power and, because the sag fell below the required voltage specification, the chiller plant's protective logic powered the chillers down and locked them out to protect the mechanical equipment. This chiller lock-out was a by-design protective response, not a fault in itself. (The Register, quoting Microsoft's RCA, describes the same event as switching the datacenter to generator power and overloading suppressors on the mechanical cooling system, shutting it down.)

The proximate root cause of customer impact was not the lightning strike but the failure of cooling redundancy to take over. Under the standard design, the Mechanical/Electrical/Plumbing (MEP) management control system automatically invokes a redundant cooling system until the chiller plant recovers — automation that had withstood similar events in many Microsoft datacenters worldwide. In this specific datacenter, per Microsoft's RCA, that automatic failover had been switched to MANUAL mode following installation of new equipment for which all testing had not yet been completed. With the automatic path disabled, the only remaining safeguard was a documented manual failover that required an engineer to act on cooling alerts. Onsite engineers were simultaneously investigating multiple concurrent alarms, and the cooling alerts were not manually actioned in time. With neither automatic nor timely manual failover, datacenter temperatures rose unchecked once thermal buffers were depleted.

As temperatures climbed, infrastructure devices and servers hit thermal-integrity shutdown thresholds; but in parts of the datacenter temperatures rose so quickly that a number of storage servers and a small number of network devices were physically damaged rather than shut down cleanly (corroborated by The Register: 'storage units and network devices, were damaged'). Recovery was deliberately prolonged by a data-integrity decision: per Microsoft's RCA, Microsoft chose to recover data in place rather than fail storage over to another region, because the asynchronous nature of geo-replication would have caused limited data loss. Recovery required replacing failed hardware, migrating customer data from damaged to healthy servers, and validating integrity across many servers with substantial manual intervention, extending South Central US impact over multiple days.

The blast radius extended well beyond South Central US because of resiliency gaps in global control-plane services whose primary metadata site is South Central US. Azure Service Manager (ASM), which handles management operations for 'classic' resource types, is a global service but keeps its primary metadata site in South Central US and does not support automatic failover, so classic management operations were impaired far beyond the region (corroborated by The Register). Azure Active Directory then degraded: per Microsoft's RCA an AAD scale-ahead autoscale operation depended on the ASM API and could not complete, QoS throttling engaged as sites neared safe-utilization limits (producing authentication failures/timeouts — the throttling and timeouts are corroborated by The Register), and an Office-client aggressive-retry bug amplified load. Microsoft's RCA also states the Azure status page itself, with non-optimized auto-scale, returned intermittent HTTP 500 errors during the traffic surge.

SUMMARY: the lightning-induced voltage sag was the trigger; the chiller lock-out was a by-design protective response; the true root cause was that redundant cooling failover had been left in manual mode (pending completion of testing after new-equipment installation) and the corresponding cooling alerts were not manually actioned amid competing alarms, letting temperatures rise fast enough to physically damage storage and network hardware. Insufficient resiliency and lack of automatic failover in dependent global services (ASM, AAD) and the status page then turned a single-datacenter cooling failure into a broad, multi-service incident.

SOURCING NOTE: Microsoft published an official RCA for this incident on its Azure status-history page; in this verification pass that original page could not be re-fetched (archive.org blocked to the fetcher, live status page rotated to current incidents), so the account rests on Microsoft's RCA as relayed and directly corroborated on its central mechanism by The Register. Precise items still resting solely on Microsoft's RCA (manual-mode cause, the 30-minutes-earlier sibling-datacenter manual failover, the Sept-7 08:40 UTC full-mitigation endpoint, the AAD/ASM-API autoscale chain, the Office-client retry bug, and the status-page 500s from ~12:30 UTC) should be treated as officially-stated-but-not-independently-re-verified here.

title: Azure South Central US: Lightning-Induced Cooling Loss and Automated Integrity Shutdown (September 2018)
text:
The failure chain runs from an electrical transient to thermal hardware damage to a control-plane cascade. Physically, lightning near the South Central US region induced voltage sags and swells on utility feeds; at ~08:42 UTC one datacenter saw a large swell immediately followed by a large sag that dropped below the chiller plant's required voltage specification, and by design the chillers powered down and locked out to protect the mechanical equipment. The Register (quoting Microsoft) adds that the same event drove the datacenter onto generator power and overloaded suppressors on the mechanical cooling system, shutting it down.

The critical control-system detail is the cooling-failover state. Normally the MEP management control system detects loss of the primary chiller plant and automatically invokes a redundant cooling system to hold temperature until the chillers recover. Per Microsoft's RCA, in this facility that automation had been switched to manual mode after new equipment was installed and before all testing was complete, leaving only a documented manual failover requiring an engineer to act on cooling alerts. Microsoft's RCA states that same manual procedure had been executed successfully in a sibling South Central US datacenter about 30 minutes earlier, but in the impacted datacenter engineers were saturated by multiple simultaneous alarms and the cooling alerts were not actioned.

With neither automatic nor manual failover engaging, there was no heat rejection while IT load continued dissipating power, so thermal buffers depleted and temperatures rose rapidly (The Register: 'as its thermal buffers were depleted, temperatures rose, and a shutdown started'). Servers and infrastructure devices carry thermal-integrity shutdown thresholds intended to power equipment off before damage; in parts of this datacenter the rate of rise outpaced that protection and a number of storage servers plus a small number of network devices sustained physical damage. That physical damage is what made recovery slow: components had to be replaced, customer data migrated from damaged to healthy servers, and integrity validated with substantial manual intervention. Per Microsoft's RCA, Microsoft deliberately declined a cross-region storage failover because geo-replication is asynchronous and failing over would have caused limited data loss, prioritizing integrity over rapid availability. (The exact full-mitigation timestamp for South Central US in the reconstruction — 08:40 UTC Sept 7 — could not be re-verified this session; The Register cites 0005 UTC on 6 September for recovery of a badly-impacted service.)

The broad blast radius is a control-plane resiliency story. ASM, the management endpoint for 'classic' resource types, keeps its primary metadata site in South Central US and — despite being a global service — supports no automatic failover, so classic management operations degraded well beyond the region (corroborated by The Register). Azure Active Directory then failed in a dependency cascade per Microsoft's RCA: its scale-ahead autoscale operation depended on the ASM API and could not complete because ASM could not process service-management operations; as AAD nodes approached safe-utilization limits, QoS throttling engaged and produced authentication failures and timeouts (throttling/timeouts corroborated by The Register); and a bug causing aggressive retry logic in Office clients amplified offered load. Separately, per Microsoft's RCA the Azure status-page web app, with non-optimized auto-scale, could not scale to incident traffic and returned intermittent HTTP 500 errors from ~12:30 UTC. Items attributed to Microsoft's RCA above (manual-mode cause, sibling-datacenter 30-minutes-earlier failover, asynchronous-geo-replication decision, AAD/ASM-API autoscale chain, Office-client retry bug, status-page 500s, and the Sept-7 endpoint) rest on Microsoft's published post-mortem, which could not be independently re-fetched in this pass; the electrical event, cooling-suppressor shutdown, thermal progression, storage/network damage, and ASM-no-automatic-failover are additionally corroborated by The Register.

title: Azure South Central US: Lightning-Induced Cooling Loss and Automated Integrity Shutdown (September 2018)
text: Failure mechanism: environmental disturbance to protective shutdown: The incident was initiated entirely outside the software stack. Lightning from a high-energy storm near San Antonio disturbed the utility supply: The Register's account of Azure's RCA describes a strike at 08:42 UTC that forced one datacenter onto generator power and overloaded surge suppressors on the mechanical cooling system, while the official VSTS postmortem frames the cause as voltage sags (undervoltage dips) and swells (overvoltage transients) that reached the facility electrical distribution and impaired the cooling plant. With heat rejection degraded, rack and hall temperatures rose toward limits that threaten silicon, storage media, and power electronics. At that point the datacenter's automated integrity procedures did their job: rather than let equipment cook, they orchestrated a structured power-down of critical hardware. The customer-visible outage was therefore a deliberate, designed consequence of a working protection system responding to an environmental input, not a defect in the servers themselves.

title: Azure South Central US: Lightning-Induced Cooling Loss and Automated Integrity Shutdown (September 2018)
text: Why it cascaded beyond the region: A physical event in one region became a broad service outage because of where state lived and how services were coupled. VSTS Scale Units and a set of user profiles were hosted in South Central US with no zonal or cross-region escape hatch, so the power-down directly took those services down. From there, tight service-to-service coupling widened the blast radius: the Marketplace dependency reached globally, and failed Marketplace calls cascaded into Dashboards, which became unavailable even for users far from Texas. Circuit breakers on some service-to-service calls (notably to the User service) were not scoped to contain failures, so instead of degrading gracefully the system propagated errors. A localized cooling loss thus radiated into a broad set of services (on the order of forty per contemporaneous reporting) and global surfaces.

title: Azure South Central US: Lightning-Induced Cooling Loss and Automated Integrity Shutdown (September 2018)
text: Recovery trajectory and its asymmetry: Recovery split into very different timescales. Restoring the physical layer, utility power and cooling, took roughly nine hours (per Data Center Dynamics). But bringing services back safely took far longer: VSTS primary recovery ran about twenty-one hours, and the official VSTS incident did not close until 00:05 UTC on 6 September, spanning the window from 09:45 UTC on 4 September (~38 hours). Broader Azure recovered more slowly still: the majority of services were back by 11:00 UTC on 5 September, but full mitigation was not declared until 08:40 UTC on 7 September. That asymmetry reflects the cost of a structured power-down: storage and compute must be powered up in a controlled, integrity-checked sequence, data consistency validated, and dependent services re-sequenced. A separate ~2-hour Release Management incident during recovery underscores how fragile the system remained mid-restoration. Because failover had not been exercised, recovery hinged on the region physically returning rather than on shifting load elsewhere.

title: Azure South Central US: Lightning-Induced Cooling Loss and Automated Integrity Shutdown (September 2018)
text: Organizational and systemic factors: The postmortem's seven remediation items read as an admission that resilience was under-invested relative to the single-region design: move to Availability Zones, add asynchronous cross-region replication, regularly exercise cross-region failover using Microsoft's own organization, add cross-region redundancy for internal tooling, fix the Dashboards/Marketplace regression, correct circuit-breaker scoping, and close fault-injection gaps. Collectively they point to a systemic gap between architectural intent and tested reality, failover paths that existed on paper but were not routinely proven, and coupling that had never been stress-tested against a full regional loss. Microsoft's own framing, the longest VSTS outage in the service's history, signals the severity these gaps produced.

title: Azure South Central US: Lightning-Induced Cooling Loss and Automated Integrity Shutdown (September 2018)
text: Cross-incident pattern: This event fits a recurring cloud-outage archetype: a facility-layer trigger (here, a lightning-induced power-quality disturbance disabling cooling) exposes software-layer single-region dependencies and under-tested failover, and the true outage duration is dominated by the careful, sequenced recovery rather than the initial fault. It also illustrates the double-edged nature of automated protection: the same integrity shutdown that saves hardware guarantees an outage if higher layers cannot absorb a region loss. The durable lesson, echoed across many large-provider postmortems, is that regional isolation, exercised failover, and correctly scoped fault containment, not facility perfection, are what keep an environmental event from becoming a global service outage.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text: On the morning of Saturday 27 May 2017, an engineer working inside British Airways' Boadicea House data centre in West London disconnected a power supply and then reconnected it in an uncontrolled, unplanned manner. The resulting surge physically damaged servers and bypassed the site's backup generators and batteries. Although the BoHo site itself was without power for only about 15 minutes, the physical damage plus a failed failover to the secondary data centre escalated a brief electrical fault into a multi-day service outage. British Airways grounded all flights at Heathrow and Gatwick, affecting roughly 75,000 passengers and as many as 672 flights. IAG later confirmed a loss of about £58m. No formal operator postmortem was ever published; BA sued its facilities supplier CBRE and the dispute settled in February 2019 with no admission of liability.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text:
No authoritative or adjudicated root cause was ever published for the 27 May 2017 British Airways outage at the Boadicea House (BoHo) core data centre near London Heathrow. Every root-cause account on record originates from the operator side (IAG/BA), was disputed by the facilities manager (CBRE), and the litigation that would have tested the competing accounts was resolved without any published judicial finding on cause. The reconstruction below reflects the best-corroborated operator account, with disputed and unverified points flagged.

TRIGGER (human/operational). Per the leaked internal explanation attributed to IAG Group IT head Bill Francis, an Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) feeding the BoHo core data centre was "over-ridden" on the Saturday morning, which "resulted in the total immediate loss of power to the facility, bypassing the backup generators and batteries" (The Register; the same "bypassing the backup generators and batteries" line appears in the leaked IAG email reported by Network World). IAG CEO Willie Walsh framed the same trigger in human terms - an engineer disconnected a power supply - which BA later characterised in its High Court claim as an "unauthorised reconnection of servers after they had been accidentally unplugged from the power supply by an engineer" (ch-aviation). The two operator descriptions are consistent in outcome: an immediate, total loss of power to the facility.

WHY THE SAFEGUARDS DID NOT CARRY THE LOAD. The defining feature is that the redundant power infrastructure did not carry the load: the internal account states the loss occurred while "bypassing the backup generators and batteries." Rather than transferring seamlessly to battery-backed UPS output and generator power, the facility went fully dark. Contemporary reporting indicated the external grid supply was not the cause and the fault lay inside the facility's own power chain; however, the specific National Grid / SSE statements sometimes cited for this point could not be independently re-verified in this review and should be treated as reported, not confirmed.

PROPAGATION - THE DAMAGE-CAUSING EVENT. The outage itself did not destroy the hardware; the uncontrolled RESTORATION did. "After a few minutes of this shutdown of power, it was turned back on in an unplanned and uncontrolled fashion, which created physical damage to the system" (The Register). A BA spokesperson restated the mechanism: "There was a loss of power to the U.K. data center, which was compounded by the uncontrolled return of power, which caused a power surge taking out our IT systems" (Network World). The causal weight sits on "uncontrolled": restoring power to a large IT load without proper sequencing produced a surge that physically damaged servers and IT hardware. One unattributed technical scenario in The Register speculated that the battery and generator supplies were briefly connected in series, yielding roughly 480V instead of 240V and causing a "literal meltdown" - but this is explicitly speculation from an anonymous source and is NOT officially confirmed.

ESCALATION AND RECOVERY. Because the failure physically damaged hardware rather than merely interrupting it, recovery required repair and rebuild, extending the event into a multi-day, airline-wide disruption. The impact stranded roughly 75,000 passengers and forced about 672 flight cancellations; IAG put the cost at around EUR65 million (about USD74 million) per ch-aviation (higher £80m-plus figures cited elsewhere could not be verified here).

DISPUTED / UNRESOLVED STATUS. CBRE, the facilities manager, disputed the engineer-error account, stating at the time that "no determination has been made yet regarding the causes of the incident on May 27" (Network World). BA commissioned an independent audit whose findings were never published, and filed a claim against CBRE in the London High Court (ch-aviation). The suit was subsequently resolved; the specific settlement date and any "no admission of liability" wording could not be verified from approved sources, but no judicial ruling on cause was ever published. Accordingly, the human/operational trigger and the uncontrolled-restoration damage mechanism are the operator's account - corroborated across multiple operator statements and a leaked internal email - but never independently adjudicated.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text:
The failure mechanism, as described by the operator, is a two-stage electrical event centred on the facility's UPS/backup power chain, with the second stage causing the actual hardware damage. All of it is the operator (IAG/BA) account plus a leaked internal email; CBRE disputed it and no independent adjudication confirmed it.

Stage 1 - loss of source without failover. A UPS feeding the BoHo core data centre was "over-ridden" (Walsh's version: an engineer disconnected a power supply). In a properly configured N+1/2N data-centre topology, removing one source should cause an automatic transfer so the load continues on battery-backed UPS output and, for a sustained outage, on generator power. Instead the event "resulted in the total immediate loss of power to the facility, bypassing the backup generators and batteries" - the batteries and generators did not pick up the load and the facility de-energised immediately (The Register; leaked IAG email via Network World). Contemporary reporting placed the fault inside the facility's own distribution rather than upstream on the grid, but the specific National Grid / SSE 'customer side of the meter' statements could not be re-verified in this review and are treated as reported, not confirmed.

Stage 2 - uncontrolled re-energisation and surge (the damaging event). 'After a few minutes... it was turned back on in an unplanned and uncontrolled fashion, which created physical damage to the system,' and the 'uncontrolled return of power... caused a power surge taking out our IT systems.' Engineering-wise, re-applying power to a large, fully-de-energised IT load without sequencing produces a severe inrush transient - many power supplies simultaneously drawing charging/magnetising current, no staged ramp, and a potentially unstable source still stabilising. Without soft-start, staged breaker closing, inrush limiting, or an orderly transfer back onto conditioned UPS output, the resulting voltage/current transient can exceed the ratings of server PSUs and other IT hardware, producing physical rather than merely logical damage. One unattributed scenario in The Register speculated the battery and generator supplies were briefly connected in series, delivering roughly 480V instead of 240V and causing a 'literal meltdown'; this is explicitly speculation from an anonymous source, never officially confirmed.

Consequence for recovery. Because the damage was physical, systems could not simply be powered back up - damaged hardware had to be repaired/replaced and systems rebuilt, consistent with the multi-day, airline-wide disruption (about 672 cancellations, roughly 75,000 passengers stranded). None of these electrical specifics were ever independently adjudicated.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text: A brief physical fault can become a multi-day outage. The BoHo site lost power for only ~15 minutes, yet recovery took days because the surge caused physical hardware damage and the failover was defeated — time-to-recover is governed by damage and data integrity, not by fault duration.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text: Redundancy that shares a failure path is not redundancy. An active/active pair that synchronises corrupted state during an uncommanded shutdown can propagate the fault to the backup, turning a single-site incident into a total service loss.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text: Failure mechanism: a human error at the power boundary: The initiating fault was not equipment failure but human mis-operation. On the Saturday morning of 27 May 2017, a power supply at Boadicea House was disconnected and then reconnected in an uncontrolled, unplanned manner. The reconnection surge physically damaged servers and bypassed the backup generators and batteries entirely. This account is dual-sourced — a leaked IAG internal email carried by the BBC and Willie Walsh on the record — and it resolves the early 'defective UPS' versus 'working perfectly' contradiction: the equipment did its job; a person operating it did not. A single technical outlet (The Register) offers a plausible physical scenario in which the restoration briefly connected battery and generator supply in series to the rack bus, feeding servers 480V instead of 240V and causing a literal meltdown. This remains a hypothesis consistent with the confirmed physical damage rather than an established fact.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text: Why it cascaded: redundancy defeated by shared state: The most consequential aspect is that BoHo itself was down for only about a quarter of an hour, yet service was lost for days. The bridge from a 15-minute fault to a multi-day outage runs through two amplifiers. First, the surge caused physical hardware damage, so recovery required hardware remediation, not a restart. Second, the failover did not save the service. The leading hypothesis is that the uncommanded shutdown synchronised corrupted data from BoHo into the secondary data centre, populating it with bad data and crashing the dependent systems — a shared-fault mode in which the backup inherited the primary's corruption. The Sunday 28 May symptom of customers seeing stale booking data offers weak independent corroboration that data integrity and replication were affected.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text: Recovery and impact: a dual-hub grounding: Because the failover could not carry the load and hardware was physically damaged, British Airways grounded all flights at Heathrow and Gatwick. On the Saturday, BA initially cancelled flights until 18:00 BST and then extended the window; an aviation expert forecast three to four days of disruption. As many as 672 flights were grounded and roughly 75,000 passengers affected — the passenger figure cross-checked across DCD's settlement reporting and the IAG/BBC account, while the specific flight count rests on a single outlet. Recovery took on the order of two to three days, with operations normalising around Monday 29 May. IAG later confirmed the financial impact at about £58m (~$74.6m), covering passenger compensation (under the EU261 schedule of EUR250/EUR400/up to EUR600) and lost business; higher press figures of $100m and up to £150m were never reconciled to an audited total.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text: Organisational and systemic factors: The incident exposed governance gaps as much as engineering ones. The engineer was authorised to be in the data centre but not authorised to do what he did, indicating that physical access and permitted-action scope were not separated or interlocked. There was no gate to stop an uncontrolled reconnection of a hazardous power source. The blame allocation was never technically settled: BA sued facilities supplier CBRE roughly 18 months later, and the dispute settled on 11 February 2019 with no admission of liability, an undisclosed amount, and no jointly agreed root cause. Critically, no formal operator or regulatory postmortem was ever published, so the entire mechanism narrative rests on press attribution and a leaked internal email — a transparency deficit for an outage of national significance.

title: British Airways Boadicea House Power Surge: A 15-Minute Fault That Grounded Heathrow and Gatwick for Days
operator: British Airways (IAG); data-centre facility management by CBRE
text: Cross-incident pattern: the small-fault, large-blast-radius archetype: This event is a canonical example of a category where a minor, brief, human-triggered fault produces an outsized outage because designed protections are bypassed and redundancy shares a failure path. The signature elements — human error during a maintenance/restoration action, backup power bypassed, and a failover that inherits corruption rather than isolating it — recur across major data-centre incidents. The lesson generalises: resilience is determined less by the redundancy that exists on paper than by whether the failure modes of the primary and backup are genuinely independent, and by whether hazardous human actions at the power boundary are procedurally gated. Here, both assumptions broke at once.

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: On 18 November 2025 an 11:05 UTC ClickHouse database permissions change exposed r0-database table metadata alongside the default database. A Bot Management feature-file generator ran a metadata query over system.columns with no database filter, which then returned duplicated column rows and more than doubled the feature file's size past a hardcoded 200-feature preallocation limit (normal usage ~60 features). When the oversized file propagated network-wide, Cloudflare's FL2 proxy module panicked on a Rust unwrap of an Err value, causing core traffic to return 5xx errors. Customer impact began at 11:28 UTC; responders first suspected a DDoS/Workers KV problem before identifying the config file, deployed a correct file globally at 14:30 UTC, and fully restored all operations by 17:06 UTC.

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text:
TRIGGER. At 11:05 UTC on 18 November 2025 Cloudflare deployed a permissions change to a ClickHouse database cluster to make previously-implicit access to underlying table metadata explicit: "Since users already have implicit access to underlying tables in r0, we made a change at 11:05 to make this access explicit." The change was rolled out gradually across the cluster, so at any moment some nodes had the new explicit grants and others did not.

MECHANISM. A query that runs every five minutes generates the "feature" configuration file consumed by the Bot Management machine-learning model. That query enumerates column metadata from ClickHouse system tables but does not filter by database name. Before the change, implicit access meant it effectively returned a single logical set of columns. After explicit grants propagated, the same unfiltered query also matched metadata for underlying tables in the r0 database and "started returning 'duplicates' of columns because those were for underlying tables stored in the r0 database," so "the response now contained all the metadata of the r0 schema effectively more than doubling the rows in the response."

SAFEGUARD THAT DID NOT HOLD. The Bot Management runtime preallocates memory against a fixed feature-count bound: "the Bot Management system has a limit on the number of machine learning features that can be used at runtime. Currently that limit is set to 200, well above our current use of ~60 features." The oversized, duplicate-laden file pushed the feature count past 200. Rather than being rejected gracefully, on the newer Rust-based FL2 proxy the loading code hit an Err result and called unwrap() on it, panicking the worker thread: "thread fl2_worker_thread panicked: called Result::unwrap() on an Err value." A panicked worker cannot serve the request, so FL2 returned HTTP 5xx. The size cap was a hard limit whose breach was not handled defensively at the point of consumption.

BLAST RADIUS BY ENGINE VERSION. Impact differed by proxy generation but the legacy engine was NOT cleanly isolated: "Customers deployed on the new FL2 proxy engine, observed HTTP 5xx errors. Customers on our old proxy engine, known as FL, did not see errors, but bot scores were not generated correctly." FL therefore avoided 5xx but produced wrong/zero bot scores, which could cause customer bot rules to mis-fire. Migration status acted as an accidental partial boundary, not a designed failover.

PROPAGATION. "The larger-than-expected feature file was then propagated to all the machines that make up our network." Because generation ran every five minutes and the permissions rollout was only partial, some cycles produced a good file and others a bad one: "every five minutes there was a chance of either a good or a bad set of configuration files being generated and rapidly propagated," so the system "would recover and then fail again," obscuring the cause.

DETECTION AND RECOVERY. First errors were observed at 11:28 UTC; an automated test detected the issue at 11:31 and an incident call was created at 11:35. Diagnosis was hindered by the good/bad oscillation and by Cloudflare's own status page going down, which led "some of the team diagnosing the issue to believe that an attacker may be targeting both our systems as well as our status page." Cloudflare later stated: "The issue was not caused, directly or indirectly, by a cyber attack or malicious activity of any kind." A Workers KV and Cloudflare Access bypass was implemented at 13:05; rollback of the Bot Management file became the focus at 13:37; creation and propagation of new files was stopped at 14:24; a correct file was deployed globally at 14:30; and all services were resolved with impact ending at 17:06 UTC. Cloudflare called it "Cloudflare's worst outage since 2019."

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text:
The failure chain is configuration-data corruption propagating into a code path that assumed well-formed input. Cloudflare's Bot Management uses a machine-learning model that ingests a "feature" configuration file, regenerated every five minutes by a query against a ClickHouse cluster.

The query enumerates column metadata from ClickHouse system tables to assemble the feature list but does not filter by database name. Under the prior implicit-access model the query effectively returned one set of relevant columns. The 11:05 UTC change ("we made a change at 11:05 to make this access explicit") granted explicit access to underlying table metadata; ClickHouse then also surfaced metadata for the underlying tables in the r0 database. With no database-name predicate, the query "started returning 'duplicates' of columns because those were for underlying tables stored in the r0 database," so "the response now contained all the metadata of the r0 schema effectively more than doubling the rows in the response."

The generated feature file therefore roughly doubled in row count. The runtime preallocates memory against a fixed feature bound: "the Bot Management system has a limit on the number of machine learning features that can be used at runtime. Currently that limit is set to 200, well above our current use of ~60 features." Doubling from ~60 pushed the count past 200. On FL2 — Cloudflare's newer Rust-based proxy engine — the code loading the feature file encountered the condition as an Err result and called Result::unwrap() on it, triggering a panic: "thread fl2_worker_thread panicked: called Result::unwrap() on an Err value." A panicked worker thread cannot serve the request, so FL2 returned HTTP 5xx.

The legacy FL proxy did not emit 5xx but was not cleanly isolated: "Customers on our old proxy engine, known as FL, did not see errors, but bot scores were not generated correctly," meaning FL-served traffic received wrong/zero bot scores that could cause customer bot rules to mis-fire. Because the ClickHouse permissions rollout was gradual, only some nodes generated the oversized file at first; the five-minute regeneration cycle therefore alternated between valid and invalid files, each rapidly propagated network-wide, producing the recover-then-fail oscillation that obscured the cause and briefly led responders to suspect an attack (compounded by the coincidental failure of Cloudflare's own status page).

Recovery required halting generation and propagation of new files (14:24 UTC), substituting a known-good earlier file and deploying a correct file globally (14:30 UTC), following an earlier Workers KV / Cloudflare Access bypass (13:05) and rollback focus (13:37); all services were resolved at 17:06 UTC. Cloudflare characterized the event as its "worst outage since 2019" and stated it "was not caused, directly or indirectly, by a cyber attack or malicious activity of any kind."

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: Unfiltered query lacking a database-name predicate: the feature-file generation query selected column metadata from ClickHouse system tables without filtering by database name, leaving it latently exposed to returning duplicate rows the moment the underlying r0 tables' metadata became visible.

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: Non-defensive consumption of a size-bounded input: the FL2 proxy relied on a hard 200-feature cap (against ~60 in use) but handled a breach with an unhandled Rust panic (unwrap() on an Err) rather than validating the file and degrading gracefully, converting a bad configuration input into customer-facing HTTP 5xx errors.

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: Partial/gradual permissions rollout across ClickHouse nodes: because explicit grants were applied progressively, some nodes produced good files and some bad ones, creating the every-five-minute good/bad oscillation that masked the cause and made the system appear to recover and then fail repeatedly.

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: Failure mechanism: The outage was a data-poisoning failure, not an infrastructure or capacity failure. A routine permissions change altered what a metadata query could see, and an unqualified SELECT over system.columns began returning duplicate column rows drawn from both the r0 and default databases. The Bot Management feature-file generator serialized those duplicated rows into a feature file that more than doubled in size. Every input on this path was individually valid - the query ran, the file was produced, propagation succeeded - yet the composed result violated a downstream invariant: a hardcoded 200-feature preallocation ceiling in the FL2 proxy against a normal load of about 60 features.

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: Why it cascaded: The proxy responded to the oversized file with a Rust panic - an unwrap on an Err value in the fl2_worker_thread - rather than rejecting or clamping the input. Because the FL2 core proxy sits on the request-serving path for a large fraction of Cloudflare-fronted traffic, that panic translated directly into 5xx errors globally. The blast radius widened because independent-seeming services shared this core path: Workers KV, Cloudflare Access, and dashboard login (through its Turnstile dependency) all degraded together, which both amplified user-visible impact and actively misled responders into chasing a Workers KV problem.

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: Detection, diagnosis and recovery: Automated testing flagged the problem within about three minutes of customer impact (11:28 -> 11:31 UTC) and an incident call opened at 11:35, so detection was fast. Diagnosis was not: symptoms resembled a DDoS and centered on Workers KV, and roughly two hours passed before attention shifted to the Bot Management config file at 13:37 UTC. Recovery then proceeded in stages - service bypasses at 13:05, halting propagation of new files at 14:24, deploying a correct file globally at 14:30 (main impact resolved), restoring the dashboard by scaling control-plane concurrency around 15:30, and full restoration at 17:06 UTC. The staged recovery shows the value of both a stop-the-bleeding step (halt propagation) and a fix-forward step (deploy good config).

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: Organizational and systemic factors: Three systemic patterns stand out. First, Cloudflare trusted its own generated configuration files on ingestion rather than validating them like user input - a control/data-plane boundary gap where internal artifacts bypass the scrutiny external ones receive. Second, a permissions change in one system (ClickHouse) propagated consequences into an unrelated pipeline (Bot Management), indicating change-review that did not account for cross-system metadata visibility. Third, the absence of an apparent canary or health-gate on feature-file publish meant there was no staged rollout to catch the bad file before it reached the whole network. Cloudflare's four committed remediations map directly onto these gaps, though none were published with owners, dates, or completion status.

title: Cloudflare Global Outage: Oversized Bot Management Feature File (November 18, 2025)
text: Cross-incident pattern: This incident fits a recurring class of large-provider outages in which the trigger is a bad configuration or data push rather than hardware or attack, and the damage comes from a hard failure mode plus a shared dependency that concentrates blast radius. The distinctive lesson here is the unqualified-query defect: a query that is correct under one schema/permissions context silently produces poisoned output under another. Combined with fail-closed hard limits (a panic instead of graceful degradation) and network-wide propagation without canarying, a small, well-intentioned permissions change escalated into a multi-hour global outage affecting many of the world's most-used services.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: On 2 November 2023 a Portland General Electric (PGE) unplanned maintenance event dropped one of two independent utility feeds into Flexential's PDX-04 data center near Hillsboro, Oregon. Roughly three hours later a ground fault on a 12,470-volt PGE transformer triggered protective systems that, by design, shut down fast — but the same protective trip also shut down all ten of PDX-04's generators, which were unusually running in parallel with the surviving utility feed. UPS batteries meant to bridge to generator power began failing after only about four minutes, and the entire facility went dark. Cloudflare's control plane and analytics ran primarily across three Hillsboro-area data centers on an assumption that any one could fail, but two critical log-processing services (Kafka and ClickHouse) existed only in PDX-04 and had dependents in the supposedly highly-available cluster; PDX-04 also held more than a third of the HA cluster and Cloudflare's largest analytics cluster. That hidden single-site dependency — a failure mode Cloudflare had never tested by fully taking PDX-04 offline — broke the redundancy design. Cloudflare's non-automated failover to European disaster-recovery sites was slow, and cold-start recovery of servers and services ran into 4 November.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text:
The November 2, 2023 Cloudflare control-plane and analytics outage originated not inside Cloudflare's network but in the electrical infrastructure of the Flexential PDX-04 colocation facility near Hillsboro, Oregon — one of three Oregon data centers on which Cloudflare's control plane and analytics run active-active. PDX-04 was the largest of the three, housing Cloudflare's largest analytics cluster and more than a third of its high-availability-cluster machines.

The trigger was utility-side: at 08:50 UTC, Portland General Electric (PGE) had an unplanned maintenance event that took down one of the facility's power feeds. This should have been survivable — the facility has multiple feeds with some level of independence, plus ten on-site generators (inclusive of redundant units) rated to carry full load. Instead a sequence of atypical operational decisions and hidden dependencies produced a full facility power loss.

Flexential failed the facility over to generator power but, counter to best practice, did not notify Cloudflare, so Cloudflare had no early warning the site was degraded. More consequentially, Flexential ran the remaining utility feed and the generators simultaneously rather than isolating onto generators — an arrangement Cloudflare called 'unusual.' Cloudflare notes Flexential participated in a PGE program called DSG (Dispatchable Standby Generation), under which the utility can run a data center's generators to help supply the grid and, in exchange, helps maintain the generators and supplies fuel; Cloudflare could find no record of ever being informed of this participation. The precise mechanism coupling the running utility feed and generators is therefore inferred by Cloudflare, not confirmed by any official Flexential or PGE root-cause document.

At approximately 11:40 UTC a ground fault developed on a PGE transformer at PDX-04. Because the utility feed and generators were running together, the protective trip did not merely isolate the utility side — it shut down all ten generators. Both primary generation sources were now offline together, and the facility fell back on its UPS battery banks, designed only to bridge the brief gap for a generator restart. The batteries, supposedly sufficient for roughly ten minutes, started to fail after only about four minutes based on Cloudflare's observation of its own equipment; there is no confirmed official explanation from Flexential or PGE for the shortfall. Cloudflare's two routers connecting PDX-04 to the outside world went offline at 11:44 UTC (Cloudflare's first indication of a problem), and complete facility power loss followed around 12:00 UTC.

Recovery was slowed by facility-side conditions: generators required a manual physical restart; electronic access-control/badge systems were down because they too depended on facility power; the overnight shift was only security plus a single unaccompanied technician who had been on the job for a week; and when Flexential attempted to re-power Cloudflare's circuits the circuit breakers were found to be faulty (cause unclear) and had to be replaced. Flexential first acknowledged the issue to Cloudflare at 12:28 UTC and restarted generators at 12:48 UTC.

Finally, the blast radius was widened by a latent flaw in Cloudflare's own design. PDX-04 was meant to be one of three redundant facilities such that any single-site loss would be transparent, but two critical services — Kafka and ClickHouse, which process logs and power analytics — ran only in PDX-04 while high-availability-cluster services depended on them. Cloudflare had never tested fully taking the entire PDX-04 facility offline, so these hard dependencies went undiscovered and failover was not clean. Cloudflare decided to fail over to disaster recovery at 13:40 UTC, brought first services up on DR at 13:43 UTC, and reached DR stability at 17:57 UTC. Clean utility power was confirmed at 22:48 UTC on November 2, but full restoration was not completed until 04:25 UTC on November 4. In short, an ordinary utility maintenance event escalated into total facility power loss via an atypical generator/utility co-running configuration, a transformer ground fault that tripped all generators, a UPS bank that failed far short of its rating, faulty breakers, and slow manual recovery — while Cloudflare's control plane and analytics failed to ride through it because untested single-facility dependencies defeated the intended three-site redundancy.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text:
The failure cascaded through four layers of the power-delivery and redundancy stack, each of which was supposed to arrest it and each of which was defeated.

Layer 1 — Utility feeds. PDX-04 has multiple feeds with some level of independence (Cloudflare's careful wording — it does not claim full independence, nor state an exact count). At 08:50 UTC an unplanned PGE maintenance event removed one feed. One feed remaining should have been sufficient, so this was a survivable single-feed loss, yet Flexential initiated a transfer to generator power.

Layer 2 — Generators. PDX-04 has ten generators (inclusive of redundant units) rated to carry full load. In a correct transfer the facility isolates load onto generators (or onto the surviving feed), keeping the sources electrically separated so a fault on one cannot propagate to the other. Instead Flexential ran the remaining utility feed and the generators at the same time — an 'unusual' arrangement Cloudflare tentatively attributes to PGE's DSG (Dispatchable Standby Generation) program. Because the fleet and the feed were coupled, when a ground fault developed on a PGE transformer at PDX-04 at ~11:40 UTC, the protective measure that responded shut down all ten generators rather than isolating only the faulted utility side. A ground fault is an unintended current path to earth; protective relays trip to prevent equipment damage and personnel hazard, but here the protection took the entire generation capability offline. The precise protection/interlock design is not confirmed by any official Flexential source. Both generation sources — utility and generators — were now dead together.

Layer 3 — UPS batteries. The UPS banks carry load for the short bridge between loss of source power and restoration of generation, supposedly ~10 minutes here, and are the last automated safeguard. In this event they started to fail after only about four minutes (per Cloudflare's observation of its own gear losing power) and then depleted, with complete facility power loss around 12:00 UTC. Whether the shortfall owed to battery health, state of charge, load, or the abnormal preceding switching sequence is not established by any official Flexential/PGE root-cause report; the ~4-minute figure is Cloudflare's empirical observation. The practical effect was that a safeguard meant to buy ~10 minutes for a manual restart delivered under half that — Cloudflare's two edge routers connecting PDX-04 externally went dark at 11:44 UTC, its first indication of the problem.

Layer 4 — Cloudflare application redundancy. Cloudflare's control plane and analytics run active-active across three Hillsboro-area data centers, continuously syncing so a single-site loss should be transparent. The defeating flaw was a hidden dependency graph: two critical services, Kafka and ClickHouse (log processing and analytics), ran only in PDX-04, while services on the nominally high-availability cluster depended on them. Cloudflare had never tested fully taking the entire PDX-04 facility offline, so this coupling went undiscovered; when PDX-04 lost power those dependencies became unavailable and failover was not clean. Recovery required a deliberate cutover to disaster-recovery sites (decided 13:40 UTC, first services up 13:43 UTC, stable 17:57 UTC), further slowed on the facility side by a manual generator restart, downed badge/access systems, thin overnight staffing, and circuit breakers found faulty during power-up. Generators restarted 12:48 UTC; clean utility power was confirmed 22:48 UTC on Nov 2; full restoration reached 04:25 UTC on Nov 4. The engineering lesson: redundancy is only as strong as its least-redundant hard dependency, and it is dependency mapping and full site-loss testing — not merely replica placement — that determine whether multi-site architecture actually survives a site loss.

text: Atypical facility configuration: Flexential ran the remaining utility feed and the on-site generators simultaneously rather than isolating onto generator power. No confirmed official explanation for the shortfall exists.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: Recovery obstacles — thin staffing, dependent systems, and faulty breakers: Generators needed a manual physical restart; electronic access-control/badge systems were down because they also depended on facility power; the overnight shift was only security plus one unaccompanied technician on the job a week; and when power-up was attempted the circuit breakers were discovered faulty and needed replacement — all of which delayed restoration.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: Untested single-facility dependencies in Cloudflare's own HA design: Two critical services, Kafka and ClickHouse (log processing and analytics), ran only in PDX-04 while high-availability-cluster services depended on them. Cloudflare had never tested fully taking PDX-04 offline, so these hard dependencies went undiscovered and the control plane and analytics could not cleanly fail over — turning a single-site power loss into a multi-day outage.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: Ensure the control plane running ON Cloudflare's network continues to function even if all core data centers are offline (push control-plane serving to the edge/network so it survives total core loss). (Cloudflare · Committed)

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: Test the blast radius of system failures and minimize the number of services impacted by any one failure; adopt more rigorous chaos-style testing including fully taking an entire facility (e.g. PDX-04) offline, a scenario never previously exercised. (Cloudflare · Committed)

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)

Inferred corrective expectation, not a Cloudflare-stated commitment. (Flexential (facility operator) · Corrective expectation raised by Cloudflare)

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: 'Redundant on paper' is not redundant if any critical service is single-homed: Cloudflare's three-site 'any-one-can-fail' assumption was silently invalidated by Kafka and ClickHouse living only in PDX-04 and by >1/3 of the HA cluster residing there. Redundancy claims must be enforced by dependency mapping, not assumed.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: Untested failure modes are latent outages: because Cloudflare had never exercised a full PDX-04 blackout, the single-site dependencies stayed hidden until a real, worst-case event surfaced them all at once. Game-day / chaos testing that actually kills a whole facility is the only way to prove blast radius.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: Facility power redundancy can share a common failure: ten full-load-rated generators provided no protection when one high-voltage ground fault's protective trip took them all down together — especially while generators were paralleled with the utility. Diverse feeds and generator counts do not guarantee independence if a single protection scheme can shed everything.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: UPS bridge time is a safety-critical assumption that must be verified, not trusted: batteries failing after ~4 minutes (versus their intended ~10-minute bridge) turned a survivable generator-restart gap into a total blackout. Battery health and true runtime need continuous validation.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: Cross-organization communication is part of the control loop: Flexential not announcing the generator failover, and taking ~44 minutes to send a first notice, left Cloudflare blind to a degraded single-point-of-power state it might otherwise have hedged against.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
text: Disaster recovery must be fast and automated to be useful: a DR failover that takes hours to stabilize (13:43 → 17:57 UTC) and a cold start running into a second day mean the control plane's resilience was theoretical, not operational.

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)

title: Cloudflare Control-Plane & Analytics Outage — Flexential PDX-04 Power Failure (Nov 2023)
