title: Google Global Authentication Outage — User ID Service Quota Collapse (Dec 14, 2020)
text: Failure mechanism — how a migration remnant zeroed a global service: The proximate trigger was not a hardware fault or traffic spike but a latent inconsistency from an incomplete migration. When the User ID Service was registered with a new quota system in October, parts of the old quota system were left running and continued to observe the service — reporting its usage as 0. Weeks later, that stale zero was treated as ground truth by automation, which reduced the account-database quota accordingly. The system was, in effect, told that a service carrying global authentication load was doing no work, and it sized capacity to match.

title: Google Global Authentication Outage — User ID Service Quota Collapse (Dec 14, 2020)
text: Why it cascaded globally: The reduced quota prevented the Paxos leader from writing, which halted credential issuance and account-metadata lookups for every Google account. Because virtually all Google products authenticate through this shared identity layer via OAuth, a single control-plane action propagated into widespread 5xx errors across independent product families at once: GCP (Console, Storage, BigQuery, GKE), Workspace (Gmail, Calendar, Meet, Docs, Drive), consumer services (YouTube, Play), and even Google Home smart speakers. The blast radius reflects architecture, not coincidence — one account database is the common dependency, so its failure is simultaneously everyone's failure.

title: Google Global Authentication Outage — User ID Service Quota Collapse (Dec 14, 2020)
text: Detection and recovery: Automated capacity alerts fired at 03:43 US/Pacific, errors began at 03:46, and engineers were paged at 03:48. Root cause was identified by 04:08 — roughly 22 minutes after onset — which is the decisive fact in keeping this under an hour. Mitigation was surgical: disable quota enforcement in one datacenter at 04:22 to confirm the fix, then roll it to all datacenters by 04:27, with error rates normalizing at 04:33. The Pacific-time sequence converts cleanly to UTC (PST = UTC-8: 03:43→11:43 alerts, 03:46→11:46 impact, 04:22→12:22 one-DC, 04:27→12:27 all-DC, 04:33→12:33 restored), and Wikipedia's independently reported UTC window (~11:45 start, ~12:33 restore, ~50 minutes) corroborates the same events, confirming the timeline's internal consistency.

title: Google Global Authentication Outage — User ID Service Quota Collapse (Dec 14, 2020)
text: Organizational and systemic factors: Three systemic conditions turned a config remnant into a global outage: automation empowered to enforce drastic capacity changes without a sanity floor; a migration process that allowed old and new quota systems to coexist and disagree; and a strongly-consistent write path (Paxos) with no graceful degradation when admission/quota was denied — a failover could not help because cluster-wide denial starved every replica's writes (inference, flagged). The official remediation emphasis on write-failure resilience implies no write fallback existed at the time.

title: Google Global Authentication Outage — User ID Service Quota Collapse (Dec 14, 2020)
text: Cross-incident pattern: This incident is a canonical shared-control-plane / identity-SPOF failure: a small, automated, seemingly-safe change in a central dependency produces disproportionate, correlated, cross-product impact. The pattern recurs across large providers — automation acting confidently on bad or stale metadata, an incomplete migration leaving inconsistent state, and a single foundational service (identity, DNS, config, or routing) whose failure defeats otherwise-independent redundancy. The mitigating counter-pattern is also visible here: fast, clear root-causing plus a pre-scoped kill-switch (disable enforcement) bounded the damage to 47 minutes.

title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
text: A latent, unguarded code path in Google Cloud's Service Control quota system — added on 2025-05-29 without error handling or feature-flag protection — was triggered on 2025-06-12 when a policy change containing unintended blank fields was inserted into the regional Spanner tables Service Control reads for policy data. The blank metadata replicated globally within seconds; regional quota checks pulled the blank fields, exercised the unprotected path, dereferenced a null pointer, and, with no error handling to contain it, the Service Control binaries crashed and entered a global crash loop. Because Service Control gates API authorization, IAM could no longer issue tokens and most Google Cloud APIs failed worldwide for several hours. The failure cascaded into downstream platforms that depend on GCP, most notably Cloudflare, whose Workers KV backend relied on the affected infrastructure.

title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
text:
On May 29, 2025, Google added a new feature to Service Control — the global control-plane component that performs per-request API management, including authorization and quota policy checks, for Google Cloud and Google Workspace products — to perform additional quota policy checks. Per Google's incident report, this change "did not have appropriate error handling nor was it feature flag protected." Because it was not feature-flag protected, it was NOT disabled by default and went live in the serving path immediately; because it lacked error handling, the new branch could not tolerate malformed policy input. The defect remained latent until data exercised the vulnerable branch roughly two weeks later.

The trigger occurred on June 12, 2025 (incident start ~10:51 PDT per the status page; a policy change was inserted shortly before). A policy change was inserted into the regional Spanner tables that Service Control uses for policies, and "this policy data contained unintended blank fields." Because quota management is global, the metadata was not rolled out gradually or region-by-region; the report states "this metadata was replicated globally within seconds," so every regional Service Control datastore received the defective policy data almost simultaneously.

The failure mechanism was deterministic and input-driven. When Service Control "regionally exercised quota checks on policies in each regional datastore," the new code path "pulled in blank fields for this respective policy change and exercised the code path that hit the null pointer causing the binaries to go into a crash loop." Lacking error handling, the null pointer was not caught as a recoverable per-request error — it crashed the process, and each restart re-read the same poisoned policy, sustaining the crash loop. Because the poisoned metadata reached every region within seconds, Service Control binaries crash-looped near-simultaneously across all regions, producing a global blast radius. With Service Control down, Google Cloud, Google Workspace and Google Security Operations products "experienced increased 503 errors in external API requests" (also described as elevated 5xx errors) worldwide.

Safeguards that could have contained the failure were absent. There was no fail-open behavior: a crash in the quota-check path took down the entire serving path rather than letting requests proceed without the check — hence Google's committed remediation to "modularize Service Control's architecture, so the functionality is isolated and fails open." Feature-flag protection that would have kept the path off by default and allowed surgical disablement was absent. Global near-instant replication of quota metadata provided no staged-rollout containment boundary. And the recovery path lacked resilience: "Service Control did not have the appropriate randomized exponential backoff implemented," so when tasks restarted after the fix they "created a herd effect on the underlying infrastructure it depends on (i.e. that Spanner table), overloading the infrastructure."

Detection was fast but recovery was slowed by that herd effect. "Within 2 minutes" SRE was triaging; "within 10 minutes, the root cause was identified and the red-button (to disable the serving path) was being put in place." The red-button was ready ~25 minutes in, and "within 40 minutes of the incident, the red-button rollout was completed, and we started seeing recovery across regions." Larger regions took materially longer: in us-central-1 the restart herd overloaded the Spanner infrastructure, and it "took up to ~2h 40 mins to fully resolve." The overall incident ended 18:18 PDT.

title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
text:
Service Control is Google's control-plane component responsible for per-request API management — including authorization and quota enforcement — for Google Cloud and Google Workspace APIs. It reads policy configuration from regional Spanner tables and, per request, exercises quota checks against the policies in that region's datastore. On May 29, 2025 an additional quota-policy-check code path was added to this hot serving path. Two safeguards were missing on that change: the report states it "did not have appropriate error handling nor was it feature flag protected." The absence of the flag meant the code was active in production and not disabled by default; the absence of error handling meant the branch assumed well-formed policy data.

The latent defect was activated by data, not by a subsequent code deploy. On June 12 a policy change carrying "unintended blank fields" was written into the regional Spanner policy tables. When Service Control "regionally exercised quota checks on policies in each regional datastore," the new code path "pulled in blank fields for this respective policy change and exercised the code path that hit the null pointer causing the binaries to go into a crash loop." Because there was no surrounding error handling, this was not a recoverable per-request error; on restart the same poisoned policy was re-read and re-evaluated, sustaining the crash loop.

The blast radius was global and near-simultaneous because of the replication topology. Quota management is globally consistent, so "this metadata was replicated globally within seconds," and each regional Service Control instance independently exercised the same fatal check against its local datastore. There was no gradual or canaried rollout of this data to act as a circuit breaker, so regions entered the crash loop at essentially the same time, and dependent APIs across Google Cloud, Workspace and Security Operations returned increased 503 / 5xx errors worldwide.

Recovery dynamics were dominated by a thundering-herd problem. The mitigation was a "red-button (to disable the serving path)," identified within 10 minutes, ready ~25 minutes in, and rolled out within 40 minutes, at which point recovery began across regions. But when Service Control tasks restarted en masse they hammered the Spanner tables they depend on. Because "Service Control did not have the appropriate randomized exponential backoff implemented," the synchronized retry storm "created a herd effect on the underlying infrastructure ... overloading the infrastructure" — most acutely in large regions such as us-central-1, which required throttling and rerouting and "took up to ~2h 40 mins to fully resolve," even though the serving-path fix rolled out within ~40 minutes. The incident ended at 18:18 PDT.

title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
text: Failure mechanism: The outage was a textbook latent-defect-meets-bad-data failure. On 2025-05-29 a quota-policy-check feature entered Service Control without error handling or a feature flag, creating a dormant, unguarded code path. It stayed inert until 2025-06-12, when a policy insert with unintended blank fields landed in the regional Spanner policy tables. When quota checks read those blank fields, they exercised the unguarded path and dereferenced a null pointer. With nothing to catch the fault, the binaries did not degrade — they crashed, and immediately restarted into the same poisoned state, producing a self-sustaining crash loop.

title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
text: Why it cascaded: Two amplifiers turned a local defect into a global outage. First, the triggering metadata replicated to every region within seconds, so there was no staggered exposure and effectively no detect-and-halt window — every region hit the null pointer at nearly the same moment. Second, Service Control sits on the authorization critical path: when it crash-looped, IAM could not issue tokens, and without tokens most Google Cloud APIs across ~70+ products failed simultaneously. The blast radius then extended beyond Google: platforms built on GCP failed downstream, most notably Cloudflare, whose Workers KV backend depended on the affected infrastructure, dragging down Durable Objects/D1, AI Gateway, Pages, Stream, Realtime and Images for roughly a 2.5-hour window (17:52–20:28 UTC; Cloudflare states the outage lasted 2h28m).

title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
text: Detection, mitigation and recovery: Mitigation was fast; full recovery was deliberately slow. Engineers identified the offending path and completed a 'red-button' rollout within ~40 minutes of the 10:51 PDT begin, after which regions recovered smaller-first. But bringing Service Control back was itself a distributed-systems hazard: restarting all tasks at once risked a herd-effect overload of the underlying infrastructure. Google therefore throttled Service Control task creation and routed traffic to multi-regional databases to shed load, which is why us-central1 — the largest region — took up to ~2h40m to fully resolve (implying ~13:31 PDT, an arithmetic estimate). The incident was declared over at 18:18 PDT, ~7h27m end-to-end, with status-page posts continuing to 23:34 PDT (12 Jun) and 16:45 PDT (13 Jun) as post-incident publication rather than new impact.

title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
text: Organizational and systemic factors: The corrective actions read as an admission that process guardrails, not just code, failed. A change reached a global, blast-radius-wide system with neither error handling nor a feature flag, and a consumer of globally-replicated data trusted that data without validating it. The remediation set — fail-open modularization, mandatory incremental feature-flagged rollout, static analysis on critical paths, an audit of all global-metadata consumers, randomized exponential backoff to blunt the recovery herd effect, and independent monitoring/communication infrastructure — targets each systemic gap. The last item is notable: it concedes that observability and customer comms shared fate with the platform, so operators were partly blind and constrained in communicating precisely when they most needed both.

title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
text: Cross-incident pattern: This incident fits a recurring cloud-era failure archetype: a single shared control-plane component (identity/authorization/quota) becomes a global single point of failure, and a benign-looking configuration or metadata change — not a hardware fault — triggers correlated, simultaneous failure everywhere at once. The same shape recurs across major providers: unvalidated input or a bad config replicates faster than humans can react, an unhandled exception converts a data problem into a crash, and deep dependency graphs turn one vendor's control-plane outage into a multi-company internet event. The durable lesson across all of them is identical to Google's own action items: validate replicated inputs, fail open on the critical path, and roll changes out incrementally with flags.

title: Google Cloud India Disruption After STT GDC Delhi Data-Center Fire
operator: Google Cloud (impacted tenant); STT GDC / Tata Communications JV (named as the third-party facility operator only by third-party reporting; not confirmed by Google)
text: On or about 5 June 2026, a fire at a third-party data-center facility in New Delhi forced an emergency power shutdown of networking equipment, isolating a non-compute Google Cloud Point of Presence (POP) in the Delhi metro and reducing available network capacity across the region. Google Cloud customers experienced elevated latency, intermittent packet loss and non-optimal routing across Delhi, Mumbai and Chennai. Google first disclosed customer impact on 9 June and worked the incident through nine status updates until resolution on 29 June, with no workaround available throughout. Recovery was gated by out-of-region capacity augmentation and, ultimately, by safety-cleared physical re-entry to the damaged site around 22-23 June. Google never named the facility, operator or ignition source; the lithium-battery/UPS attribution comes only from third-party reporting, not from Google's record.

title: Google Cloud India Disruption After STT GDC Delhi Data-Center Fire
operator: Google Cloud (impacted tenant); STT GDC / Tata Communications JV (named as the third-party facility operator only by third-party reporting; not confirmed by Google)
text:
SPECIFIC IGNITION SOURCE: Per third-party reporting (Data Center Dynamics; Outlook Business; NDTV Profit; People Matters), Delhi fire authorities located the origin in lithium battery units in a third-floor battery room of STT Delhi 2 (Next-Gen Tower, Greater Kailash-1, New Delhi; reported 1.1 MW; ST Telemedia / Tata Communications JV). A pivotal DCD detail is that the batteries "belonged to a company leasing space at the site" — i.e., a COLOCATION TENANT's own battery installation, not confirmed to be the operator's central UPS plant. This shifts ignition ownership from the operator's maintained infrastructure toward a tenant-controlled energy-storage deployment inside a shared hall. NOTE (QA): only Google's own Service Health page is independently re-verifiable at review time; the battery-origin, floor, facility-identity and tenant-ownership details rest on secondary outlets that could not be re-fetched and should be read as reported, not confirmed.

EQUIPMENT DETAIL — DISCLOSED UNCERTAINTY: The cell chemistry is reported only as generic "lithium-ion." Make, model, manufacturer, install date, age, rated capacity (kWh/Ah), BMS design, charger/charging regime, string voltage, and battery-room thermal conditions are ALL undisclosed in every public source as of the access date. No source establishes whether the cells were LFP, NMC, or another variant — a material distinction, since NMC chemistries have lower thermal-runaway onset temperatures and higher energy release than LFP.

EXACT FAILURE MECHANISM — NOT CONCLUSIVELY ESTABLISHED: A "short circuit" was cited as the suspected PRELIMINARY cause, explicitly "under investigation" (People Matters). This is consistent with lithium-ion thermal runaway seeded in a battery string, but the official cause was reported as inconclusive pending an independent root-cause analysis commissioned by STT Global (reported due ~5–7 weeks from June 23, 2026, i.e. late-July to early-August 2026). The propagation pathway, whether cell-to-cell cascade was arrested, and whether the room had thermal barriers or cell-level isolation, are unknown.

LATENT ROOT — DESIGN & PROTECTION: The more consequential root causes are architectural and detection/suppression-related, and the record is notable for its SILENCE. No public source names any in-facility fire-detection system (VESDA/aspirating, spot smoke/heat) or a sensed-alarm time; the only detection datapoint is the human emergency call to the Delhi Fire Service at ~02:45 IST. No source describes the battery room's fixed suppression (clean-agent such as FM-200/Novec-1230, inert gas, or pre-action sprinkler), whether it discharged, or why it failed. Lithium-ion thermal runaway is largely unquenchable by gaseous clean agents (which displace oxygen but do not remove runaway's self-sustaining internal heat), so any installed gas system would plausibly have been ineffective — but this is analytical inference, not confirmed fact. The documented suppression record is entirely manual: Delhi Fire Service tenders over several hours.

LATENT ROOT — SEGREGATION & REDUNDANCY: A single physical hall combined a tenant lithium battery installation, Google's peering/edge POP hardware, and other tenants' equipment (reported: Matrix Cellular, Netflix, NCR ISPs) with insufficient compartmentation; damage was confined to the third floor, but that floor concentrated enough shared infrastructure to force a metro-wide capacity cut. On the Google side, the latent root of the CLOUD disruption was topological and IS officially confirmed: the emergency de-energisation "isolat[ed] a non-compute local Point of Presence (POP) in Delhi," degrading ingress across THREE metros — a redundancy/blast-radius design gap in edge placement, NOT a compute-region (asia-south2) failure (Google Cloud Service Health, incident 5fGQt4VbkDnr3Yp8PXPr).

LATENT ROOT — REGULATORY VACUUM: MediaNama (unverifiable at review) attributes the deeper cause to India's regulatory environment: the DPDP Draft Rules mandate data localisation but set no facility fire-safety standard, redundancy requirement, or minimum-uptime obligation; data centres are treated as ordinary buildings — a systemic latent condition amplifying a single-facility fire into a national-scale digital event.

MAINTENANCE LAPSE — STATUS: No specific maintenance, inspection, BMS-calibration, charging-control, or fire-barrier-testing lapse is evidenced in any public source. That venue is the pending STT RCA, whose findings are not public. Novamesh's "force majeure" characterisation is a contractual disclaimer, not an investigative conclusion. Any maintenance root cause is therefore UNKNOWN pending the RCA — a gap this dossier flags rather than fills.

title: Google Cloud India Disruption After STT GDC Delhi Data-Center Fire
operator: Google Cloud (impacted tenant); STT GDC / Tata Communications JV (named as the third-party facility operator only by third-party reporting; not confirmed by Google)
text:
This was a cross-domain cascade in which a physical fire in a colocation tenant's battery room propagated into a hyperscaler's network-edge outage through a deliberate protective action, not through direct fire damage to cloud compute. The chain has three layers; only Layer 2 and its outcome are independently confirmed by Google's own Service Health record, while Layer 1's fire-forensics rest on secondary reporting that could not be re-fetched at review time.

LAYER 1 — THE PHYSICAL FIRE. At ~02:45 IST on 2026-06-05, lithium battery units in the third-floor battery room of STT Delhi 2 entered what fire authorities preliminarily attributed to a short circuit — the classic seed of lithium-ion thermal runaway (People Matters; DCD, unverified at review). DCD reported the batteries "belonged to a company leasing space" — a tenant, not confirmed to be the operator's UPS plant. The only detection event in the public record is the human call to the Delhi Fire Service at ~02:45 IST; whether any in-facility aspirating/spot detection alarmed earlier is undisclosed. No fixed suppression discharge is documented — a critical gap, because a battery-origin lithium fire would likely defeat gaseous clean-agent systems, which cannot remove runaway's internal self-heating. Suppression was therefore reported as entirely manual: DFS arrived "within minutes," deployed ten tenders, and fought the fire for several hours, confining it to the third floor. Reporting described destroyed server racks, collapsed ceiling panels and demolished electrical infrastructure (NDTV Profit). Two firefighters were reported injured with no fatalities (Outlook; People Matters; The Hindu) — though a later DCD report reportedly stated "no injuries," an unreconciled discrepancy this dossier flags rather than resolves.

LAYER 2 — THE PROTECTIVE DE-ENERGISATION (THE CASCADE TRIGGER) [OFFICIALLY CONFIRMED]. Per Google Cloud Service Health (incident 5fGQt4VbkDnr3Yp8PXPr): "A fire at a third-party data center facility required an emergency power shutdown of networking equipment, isolating a non-compute local Point of Presence (POP) in Delhi." This is the hinge of the whole event: the cloud impact was caused by a deliberate, safety-driven shutdown of Google's own peering/edge gear co-located in the third-party hall — NOT by fire destroying a compute region (asia-south2 is merely the Delhi region label). "Non-compute" means peering/edge/ingress rather than customer VMs.

LAYER 3 — THE METRO-SCALE PROPAGATION [OFFICIALLY CONFIRMED]. Removing that POP's capacity forced rerouting, producing "slightly elevated latency and non-optimal network routing" for traffic into Google Cloud from the Delhi, Chennai and Mumbai metro areas as demand exceeded regional capacity. One POP loss thus degraded three metros — an edge blast-radius/redundancy characteristic. Google's documented mitigations (per the status page) were: restoring Internet Edge peering capacity in Delhi, augmenting out-of-region capacity in Chennai, optimizing backbone capacity, and restoring the Delhi-Chennai and Delhi-Mumbai connections. (A secondary account (Data Center Knowledge) additionally framed the response as "migrating selected peering partners"; that phrasing is not in the official text.) Full restoration was gated on physical safety: Google could only restore all lost capacity after obtaining safety clearance, with the incident "recovered and returned to normal service as of Friday, 2026-06-26 PDT" — a ~3-week tail driven by fire/structural hazard lockout, not network engineering. Beyond Google, the same hall reportedly damaged Netflix and NCR-ISP equipment and threatened ~20 years of Matrix Cellular data, with losses in the "hundreds of crores" of rupees (The Hindu; Outlook, unverified at review). STT Global reportedly commissioned an independent RCA (due ~5–7 weeks from June 23); Novamesh (Tata Communications) reportedly framed it as force majeure.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: On 15 October 2022, a lithium-ion UPS battery on the third basement level (B3) of the SK C&C Pangyo Data Center ignited and spread, forcing firefighters and operators to cut power to the entire facility. Because tenant Kakao had concentrated core functions — including its sole authentication service — at this single site, the power cut cascaded into a nationwide outage of KakaoTalk, Daum, Kakao-linked banking, KakaoT and dozens of downstream services. Co-tenant Naver, which kept its own separate data center, was far less affected. KakaoTalk stayed down for more than 11 hours, the longest in its history, and full restoration of all Kakao services took roughly five days. The event triggered a CEO resignation, a three-way blame dispute, and South Korea's "Kakao Outage Prevention Act" mandating geographic redundancy for major platforms.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text:
TRIGGER. On 15 October 2022 at approximately 15:30 KST (오후 3시30분경), a fire broke out in the basement electrical room of SK C&C's Pangyo data center in Seongnam, South Korea. The Korean-language record states the ignition point as "지하 3층 무정전전원장치에서 발화" (ignition in the UPS at basement level 3, B3F), and ZDNet Korea's same-day report independently places the origin in the underground electrical room ("지하에 위치한 전기실에 발생한 것으로 알려졌다"). The seat of the fire was thus the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) / battery installation on the B3F electrical floor — the very equipment meant to provide backup ride-through power.

MECHANISM — WHY THE OUTAGE HAPPENED WITHOUT SERVERS BURNING. Critically, the fire did not physically destroy the tenant server halls. ZDNet Korea confirms the fire did not spread to the server/computer rooms ("화재가 서버실과 전산실까지 확산되지 않아"). The outage was instead caused by a deliberate fire-safety measure: to prevent the fire from spreading and to allow firefighters to work safely around energized electrical equipment, power to the entire building was cut ("건물 전체 전원 공급을 차단"). This building-wide de-energization — not flame or smoke damage to compute hardware — is what took the servers offline. On-site UPS/battery redundancy could not bridge the load because the UPS installation itself was the seat of the fire and the whole building was intentionally de-energized. (The frequently cited "~15:29 power cut to Kakao's zone" is not supported by the retrieved sources and is omitted here.)

WHY REDUNDANCY DID NOT ABSORB THE LOSS. The loss of a single facility should, in a properly distributed architecture, have been survivable via geographically dispersed failover. The Korean record identifies the core organizational root cause as the absence of an effective distributed data-center architecture: the facility operated as a single point of failure and Kakao's servers were insufficiently dispersed. The record is pointed that nothing had changed since a materially similar single-data-center-dependency outage a decade earlier (April 2012): "10년 전 사건이 일어났을 때 이후로 서버 분산 등의 달라진 점이 없다." Because a critical share of Kakao's core services (and other tenants including Naver) was concentrated in this one center without working cross-site failover, the single-facility power loss cascaded into a nationwide service outage.

ESCALATION AND SLOW RECOVERY. The fire was suppressed the same night at 23:46 KST, 8 hours 13 minutes after ignition ("8시간 13분 후인 그날 23시 46분에 진화되었다"). Restoring power nonetheless proved slow because the fire-damaged electrical room could not be safely re-energized immediately. Recovery therefore stretched far beyond suppression: mobile KakaoTalk was partially restored overnight, but full service restoration was not completed until 20 October 2022 ("10월 20일 23시, 모든 서비스와 기능들이 복구 완료됐다") — roughly 127 hours after the fire, one of the longest outages in the company's history. MSIT (과학기술정보통신부) coordinated the government response and Kakao co-CEO Namkoong Whon resigned over the outage (confirmed by the English Wikipedia Kakao article: "co-CEO Namkoong Whon resigned after a service outage caused by a data center fire").

SOURCING CAVEAT (unchanged and important). The B3F-UPS ignition finding and the "power-cut, not fire-damage" mechanism are drawn from ZDNet Korea (same-day) and Korean/English Wikipedia aggregations — press/tertiary sources, not a primary forensic document. The verbatim MSIT official cause-investigation report (reported published 2022-12-06) and any NFS/police final forensic conclusion (in particular whether the precise battery-ignition mechanism was conclusively determined or left undetermined) were NOT independently retrieved. The specific attribution of the forensic origin investigation to the NFS (국립과학수사연구원) and the Gyeonggi Nambu Provincial Police is not supported by the retrieved sources and should be treated as unverified. The exact ignition mechanism inside the UPS/battery installation therefore remains reported-but-not-primary-verified.

Official confirmation. Official source genuinely established this pass. The MSIT investigation press release ('디지털서비스 장애 원인 조사결과 및 시정조치 요구', 6 Dec 2022) was read via korea.kr, the official Korean-government policy-briefing portal (KOGL type-1) that republishes MSIT releases verbatim — a legitimate primary official/regulatory document, hence officialPostmortem=true. MSIT's own msit.go.kr served a maintenance/bot-block page for every request, so the ministry-hosted copy could not be read directly. The fire-origin conclusion comes from the National Forensic Service (NFS) 감정 결과 and the police+NFS+fire-authority joint on-site exam; these are official-body findings but were only accessible as verbatim Yonhap wire quotations (labeled 'press' here for honesty), since NFS/police did not publish standalone public reports. The exact reason for the battery cell's internal insulation breakdown remained officially undetermined and no criminal charges were filed as of the reporting. There was no prior detailed root cause supplied; the finalRootCause was constructed from the official findings.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text:
The Pangyo event is best understood as a small fire that caused a national outage — the damage vector was electrical de-energisation, not combustion. The fire itself was tiny in physical terms: only about 40㎡ of the 3,300㎡ B3F battery room was charred, roughly 60 battery packs were consumed, and the fire never reached the server halls. The ~32,000 Kakao servers and Naver equipment were physically intact throughout. What took them down was the whole-building power cut, executed because the fire could not be suppressed any other way.

The forensic chain runs like this. At 15:19 an aged Li-ion cell (internal short from insulation breakdown per NFS) sparked. The BMS — the layer meant to see exactly this — did not register it, holding a steady ~20°C reading through an active fire, meaning either the sensing scheme could not see cell-internal runaway or the monitoring loop had failed silently. Detection instead came from a separate automatic fire-detection loop tied to the suppression system, which triggered at 15:20, about one minute later, and discharged the gas — approximately 1,500 kg (50 kg × 30 cylinders).

The gas system activated correctly and on time but did not extinguish the fire, and this failure was physics, not malfunction. Gaseous agents asphyxiate by displacing oxygen; a Li-ion cell in thermal runaway generates heat and oxygen internally and is sealed in casing, so the agent has no gap to penetrate. Compounded by the enclosed B3F electrical room, only water — which adds a cooling effect the gas lacks — could arrest the runaway. Reporting noted that despite 1,500 kg of gas discharged, knocking down a fire over roughly 40㎡ still took about two hours.

But water and live UPS busbars are incompatible: electrocution risk. At 16:52 firefighters formally requested SK C&C cut power. Here the topology became decisive. The UPS feeding the burning B3F zone also fed the whole center, cabling ran above the batteries and had already burned through, and some UPS units were not fully partitioned from the battery room. Staff could not identify in time which zones/switches needed selective isolation, so no selective cut was possible. A whole-building shutdown was executed, instantly de-energising the Kakao/Naver fleet — "카카오 서버 전체인 3만2000대의 전원 공급이 끊겨." Firefighters arrived at 15:37 (18 minutes after the spark); main flames were knocked down about two hours after ignition (~17:19), and full extinguishment was declared at 23:46 — an 8h13m operation measured from the 15:33 report — with peak mobilization of 114 personnel and 46 apparatus. Kakao's services did not fully normalize until 127h30m later, a recovery time driven not by the fire but by the scale of restarting and re-syncing 32,000 servers with no geographic redundancy.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: A small fire, a national outage: The Pangyo incident is a textbook case of impact decoupled from physical damage. Only ~40 sqm of a 3,300 sqm battery room charred, ~60 packs burned, and flames never reached the server halls — the ~32,000 Kakao servers and Naver gear were intact throughout. The outage came entirely from the whole-building power cut needed to fight the fire safely. The lesson is that a data center's blast radius is defined by its electrical topology and its dependency graph, not by how much of it burns.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: Why gas suppression could not work: The clean-agent/halogen system discharged correctly within ~1 minute of the spark, yet the fire burned on. This was physics, not malfunction: gaseous agents extinguish by displacing oxygen, but a Li-ion cell in thermal runaway generates its own heat and oxygen and is sealed in casing, so the agent has no gap to penetrate. In an enclosed basement room, only water — which cools as well as smothers — can arrest the runaway. Reporting underscored the mismatch: ~1,500 kg of gas failed to stop a fire over roughly 40 sqm.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: The detection blind spot: The BMS, nominally the early-warning layer, reported a steady ~20C throughout an active fire and flagged no anomaly before ignition. Whether the sensing scheme simply could not see a cell-internal short or the loop had failed silently, the operational result was false assurance. Detection that is not validated against the exact failure mode it must catch — internal short and thermal runaway in an aged cell — is a control that exists on paper only.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: Topology as the amplifier: The single most consequential design choice was coupling: the UPS feeding the B3F fire zone also fed the whole center, cabling ran directly above the batteries and burned through at onset, and some UPS units were not fully separated from the battery room. When firefighters needed the power off at 16:52 to apply water, staff could not identify which switches would isolate only the fire zone, so a whole-building shutdown was the only option. Good design would have made selective isolation a labeled, drilled, minutes-long action.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: Single-site dependence and the regulatory gap: Kakao's near-total reliance on one site, with no geographic redundancy and no drills for a full power-loss scenario, turned a facility fire into a 127h30m recovery. MSIT assigned fault to both operator and tenant. Compounding it, enhanced data-center suppression requirements effective Feb 2022 were not applied retroactively to the 2016 building, leaving the highest-risk room under the weakest standard — a reminder that grandfathering legacy critical infrastructure can institutionalize the very gap that fails.

title: NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work
text: On the evening of 26 September 2025, a lithium-ion UPS battery that had been disconnected in order to be relocated to the basement of the NIRS Daejeon government data center entered thermal runaway and exploded in a server room, igniting a fire that took roughly ten hours to extinguish. When the fire broke out, all 647 government IT systems at the Daejeon headquarters were taken offline (96 of them directly destroyed, the rest shut down as a precautionary safety measure). Core national services including digital IDs, Korea Post postal banking, emergency GPS tracking, courts and tax were paralyzed, and all documents on the G-Drive cloud used by up to 30 ministries and nearly 191,000 employees were permanently lost because the repository was not backed up externally. Recovery reached 70.5 percent by 24 October and later exceeded 95 percent; the NIRS chief and three other officials were booked for causing the fire through on-duty negligence, the chief was relieved of duty, and Daejeon police raided NIRS.

title: NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work
text:
At approximately 20:20 KST on 2025-09-26 a fire broke out in the fifth-floor UPS room of the National Information Resources Service (NIRS) headquarters in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon, during work to physically relocate lithium-ion UPS batteries. Per the Korean-language record, a worker switched off the UPS lithium-ion battery power and, about 40 minutes later, sparks flew from a battery 'for an unknown reason' (미상의 이유로) and ignited the fire — so the exact ignition trigger was officially still undetermined and under forensic testing, even though the surrounding negligence was established. The RCA's framing of a confirmed 'explosion during electrical work' overstates that certainty.

Korean National Police investigators concluded the relocation was performed on batteries that were neither electrically isolated nor made energetically safe to handle, and filed professional-negligence charges. Two conditions compounded. First, although the building's main power was disconnected when the fire began, an auxiliary power system connected to the UPS battery-backup remained energized. Second, the cells were not discharged and sat at roughly 80-90% state of charge — near-maximum stored energy (experts note that the higher the charge, the greater the potential fire damage, and manufacturers recommend a low or moderate charge before moving lithium-ion batteries). Investigators found workers failed to follow safety protocols, did not use the required insulation materials, and did not fully discharge the batteries before moving them.

Human and procedural safeguards were absent: the staff were not qualified for the job and had no battery-relocation experience; the battery manufacturers were deliberately excluded to cut costs; and the work had been illegally subcontracted — the two firms that won the tender handed it to three other businesses in breach of Korean law, with the two primary contractors falsifying employment records to make the crews appear to be their own staff.

Consequences were severe because recovery redundancy was inadequate at the data layer. The 858TB 'G-Drive' — one of 96 systems completely destroyed in the fire — had no backup, reportedly because its large capacity made backup impractical, leaving government work materials effectively unrecoverable and operations 'practically at a standstill.' The fire forced NIRS to power down all 647 affected government systems; initial fire control took over 10 hours, and one worker suffered first-degree burns to the face and arm.

Five people were charged with professional negligence resulting in fire — one NIRS official, one project-management-firm worker, and three construction-company employees — with charges reported in late October 2025. Recovered batteries were undergoing disassembly testing and identical models were slated for re-creation experiments to determine the exact cause of ignition. No primary official/government or court root-cause report was available; these findings rest on press reporting of police statements, and the matter was proceeding through the criminal-justice process.

Official confirmation. This pass newly established genuine primary official sources: two Republic-of-Korea government press releases on the official korea.kr portal — MOIS ('전산실 내 리튬이온 배터리의 안전 조치' / safety measures for lithium-ion batteries inside the server room) and the National Fire Agency ('최근 대전 국가정보자원관리원 화재를 계기로' / prompted by the recent Daejeon NIRS fire). These are genuine official documents with verbatim quotes that confirm the incident and officially direct remediation at the server-room lithium-ion UPS battery, so officialPostmortem=true and flipped=true under the source-type criterion. HONEST CAVEAT: these official docs are not a full forensic postmortem — the standalone primary forensic root-cause report (National Forensic Service / National Fire Agency investigation / Daejeon Police joint probe) was NOT directly retrievable (its cause detail sits in unrendered HWP/PDF attachments; wire services Yonhap/AP/Reuters were unreachable). The crisp verbatim root-cause statements ('lithium-ion batteries powering the UPS were identified as the source'; 'blaze broke out as the UPS was being relocated to the basement'; 'explosion of lithium-ion batteries ... cited as the main cause') come from The Korea Herald (press), attributing the cause to forensic officials and the relocation-negligence focus to police. No official cause was fabricated; the official sources corroborate the cause direction and the government's remedial response rather than supplying a cell-level forensic conclusion.

title: NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work
text:
The event is a textbook demonstration of why lithium-ion energy storage in a server hall defeats the fire-protection assumptions data centers are built on. A conventional server-hall fire regime — clean-agent (inert gas or chemical clean agent) plus cautious or prohibited water application to protect equipment — is designed for combustion that needs external oxygen. A Li-ion cell in thermal runaway is self-oxidising: the decomposing cathode liberates oxygen internally, so smothering agents cannot starve it, and the reaction propagates cell-to-cell as each venting cell heats its neighbours. With the pack reported at 384 modules, once one cell failed during disconnection the runaway chained across the bank (breached.company, secondary). This is why the fire "reignited repeatedly" and why full extinguishment reportedly took ~22 hours after ignition, with initial knockdown alone taking over 10 hours — the >10h figure is verified in ko.wikipedia ("초진까지 10시간 이상이 소요되었다"), while the ~22h full-out and >160°C peak are press-derived secondary.

The suppression dilemma is the central operational lesson. The room's fixed suppression did not arrest the event. ko.wikipedia (verified) states water-based firefighting was difficult because of concern over damaging the data-storage equipment, driving the >10-hour initial knockdown. But gas/clean agent cannot quench a self-oxidising runaway, and cautious water cannot rapidly cool cascading modules. The only reliable Li-ion tactic — total immersion / copious water cooling — was the one tactic the room's mission forbade. That unresolved conflict is what this incident exposes.

The second dynamic is the de-energisation cascade. NIRS cut power to all 647 Daejeon systems ("647개 시스템"), partly a protective shutdown because the fire and response knocked out the room's HVAC/CRAC (항온항습장치); without cooling and dehumidification, running servers would overheat (ko.wikipedia, verified). So the outage was driven as much by the deliberate mass power-down and lost cooling as by flame — in a dense DC the blast radius of a single-rack event is defined by shared power and cooling topology, not the fire's physical footprint. Detection specifics (VESDA/aspirating, spot smoke/heat, or battery off-gas detection) and any automated-alarm time are NOT disclosed in any source; what is documented is a human-noticed first report at ~20:15 KST and ignition at ~20:20 (ko.wikipedia). No source indicates any battery-level gas or thermal-runaway early-warning system caught cell venting before flame — a detection gap that, for Li-ion, is the difference between a vented cell and a multi-hour fire.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: On 7 May 2026 (around 08:45 local time) a fire broke out in a rear technical compartment of NorthC's Almere data center (Rondebeltweg) that houses power infrastructure. No servers or data carriers caught fire, but the blaze burned part of the facility's power supply and the site lost power entirely — the compute survived, yet everything went dark, and NorthC ultimately had to rebuild the power plant with new transformers and UPS. (Published reporting says only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'; that BOTH the normal and standby feeds were lost is an engineering inference from the total, multi-day power loss and the full rebuild, not an official finding.) Because multiple Dutch organizations host critical systems there, the outage cascaded outward: Utrecht University, Statistics Netherlands (CBS), public-transport operator Transdev, a regional water board, research-ICT provider Surf, IBM Cloud's Amsterdam 03, and numerous GP practices all lost service. The fire was scaled down to GRIP 1 at 20:50 that evening and to GRIP 0 with the building partially released to NorthC teams at 00:35 on 8 May, kicking off a phased restoration estimated at up to 72 hours. Temporary redundant power and cooling were activated on 13 May, roughly a week after the fire. Grid power came back building-by-building over the following weeks, with Building 1's full utility-plus-standby topology targeted for 17 July 2026. The root cause remains officially undetermined; a draft cause report was only expected at end-September 2026 because the fire-damaged structure had to be secured first.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text:
SPECIFIC IGNITION SOURCE — NOT PUBLICLY DISCLOSED (investigation open). No primary or press source names the equipment that ignited: no make, model, age, or chemistry, and no failure mechanism. On day one NorthC stated plainly that nothing was yet known about the cause. NorthC commissioned an independent expert investigation, but forensic work could only begin after the severely damaged, unstable structure was secured (a demolition/investigation window of 27 July–7 August 2026), and NorthC expects only a DRAFT cause report by end of September 2026. As of the reporting window the ignition source and chemistry are genuinely unknown; any specific attribution would be fabrication.

WHAT IS FIRMLY ESTABLISHED (confirmed on the official NorthC status page) is the location and the affected system class. The fire started at the rear of the building, where the technical facilities are located, inside the emergency-power / technical room of the "Almere 1" compartment, and centred on the site's power infrastructure. The consequence set narrows the field: the transformers and UPS systems in that compartment were destroyed and the emergency electrical installation was "classified as lost" (NorthC), while no IT gear was fire-damaged (DataCenterDynamics, crawl-cited). That the destroyed plant was UPS + transformers makes two failure families physically plausible — (a) a UPS energy-storage thermal event (a VRLA or Li-ion battery string entering thermal runaway) or (b) an electrical fault in a transformer or switchgear/distribution assembly (arc flash, insulation breakdown, connection overheating). BOTH are UNCONFIRMED; no source attributes ignition to either, and this dossier asserts neither.

LATENT / SYSTEMIC ROOT (what the record supports). At the operator level the design worked as intended where it mattered for life-safety and containment: the two-compartment topology and PASSIVE fire compartmentation confined the fire to the rear power room and kept the data halls and their IT largely intact — "The fire compartmentation prevented the smoke from spreading further" and "smoke in the halls remained limited" (NorthC, verified). Where the design failed was in continuity of the affected compartment's own power train: the fire took out transformers and UPS together, i.e. primary and backup power for Almere 1 shared enough physical proximity in one technical room that a single fire destroyed the entire emergency electrical installation of that half of the site. That is a redundancy / physical-separation latent root inside Almere 1's power topology, even though inter-compartment separation (Almere 1 vs Almere 2) held.

Second — the more consequential systemic root for the outside world — the severe downstream impact was NOT caused by any NorthC fire-safety failing but by SINGLE-SITE customer architectures with no disaster-recovery failover. Transdev's regional control-centre servers had not been migrated to a backup location, so bus drivers lost communications and the in-vehicle emergency button stopped working; Utrecht University, Infomedics and the local water board carried single-site dependencies on this one facility (TNW / Computable, crawl-cited).

MAINTENANCE / INSPECTION / TESTING LATENT ROOT — NONE EVIDENCED, NOT EXONERATED. No source implicates any hot-work permit, deferred maintenance, failed test, or procedural breach at NorthC — consistent with the cause investigation still being open. Any maintenance-cause theory must be treated as unproven pending the expert report (draft due end September 2026).

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text:
The NorthC Almere site is an 11 MW facility of roughly 26,000 sqm across two buildings, split into two functionally separate power/fire compartments referred to as "Almere 1" and "Almere 2" (11 MW / 26,000 sqm figures from DataCenterDynamics, crawl-cited and not independently re-verified this pass). The fire, at approximately 08:30–08:45 on Thursday 7 May 2026, originated in the rear technical room housing Almere 1's emergency-power plant (NorthC dates the outbreak to "around 08:45"; Omroep Flevoland/TNW report ~08:30).

Two forensic facts dominate the physics. FIRST, this was an ELECTRICAL / POWER-PLANT fire, not an IT-white-space fire: damage was concentrated around the site's power infrastructure, the transformers and UPS in the Almere 1 room were destroyed, and "the emergency electrical installation was classified as lost" (NorthC, verified), while no IT gear was fire-damaged (DCD, crawl-cited). SECOND, PASSIVE containment — not active suppression — is what saved the halls: "The fire compartmentation prevented the smoke from spreading further" and "smoke in the halls remained limited" (NorthC, verified).

Two disclosure gaps must be stated honestly. DETECTION: no source discloses the detection technology, zone, or first-alarm time. What is documented is the human outcome — the building was evacuated in time with no injuries; per CEO Alexandra Schless, "All people present were evacuated from the building in time" (NorthC, verified). ACTIVE SUPPRESSION: no source states whether any automatic suppression (gaseous/clean-agent, water-mist, sprinkler) was installed in the affected power room, whether it discharged, or why it failed to hold. This is a real gap: the fire burned into the evening and was fought manually, with "brand meester" (fire under control) reported only around 20:30 — roughly 11–12 hours after outbreak (Omroep Flevoland, crawl-cited). Firefighting was severely hampered because the compartment was too unstable and too damaged to send crews inside; facade sections were demolished with cranes for access, a drone from Brabant was flown for interior imaging, and a fire truck from Lelystad Airport assisted (Omroep Flevoland / Computable, crawl-cited).

The electrical response and recovery are the best-documented portion and are confirmed against the official NorthC status page. The fire department ordered a complete datacenter shutdown. In the undamaged half, the backup generators started automatically ("De noodstroomgeneratoren in het andere deel (Almere 2) sloegen automatisch aan," Computable, crawl-cited). Almere 1, having lost its transformers and UPS, required a full temporary power train — generators, UPS, distribution units and more than 1 km of cable — activated on 13 May (about six days post-fire; NorthC confirms "temporary power May 13"). Almere 2 was reconnected to the grid on 29 May; Almere 1 was reinstated in phases (transformers/UPS reinstalled) with initial grid connection by end June and full grid operation targeted end July 2026 (all confirmed on the NorthC page). Veiligheidsregio Flevoland ran the incident at GRIP 2 with an NL-Alert advising residents to avoid smoke, close windows/doors and disable mechanical ventilation as smoke drifted south toward 't Gooi; emergency measurements found no dangerous-substance concentrations. Reported GRIP de-escalation (GRIP 2 → GRIP 1 ~20:50 on 7 May, NL-Alert withdrawn; → GRIP 0 ~00:35 on 8 May) originates with Veiligheidsregio Flevoland / Omroep Flevoland and was not independently re-verified this pass.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: What happened: At ~08:30–08:45 on 7 May 2026 a fire broke out in the rear technical room of the 'Almere 1' compartment of NorthC's Almere data center, centred on the site's power infrastructure. Everyone was evacuated in time with no injuries. Transformers and UPS in that room were destroyed and the emergency electrical installation was 'classified as lost' (NorthC, verified). The fire brigade ordered a full shutdown and fought the blaze into the evening, with 'brand meester' reported around 20:30. The ignition source and chemistry remain publicly unknown; NorthC expects only a draft cause report by end September 2026.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: Why the data halls survived: passive containment: The load-bearing safety story is passive fire compartmentation, not active suppression. Per NorthC, 'The fire compartmentation prevented the smoke from spreading further' and 'smoke in the halls remained limited.' The two-compartment topology held between Almere 1 and Almere 2, so no IT gear was fire-damaged even as the Almere 1 power room was destroyed. No source discloses whether any automatic suppression existed in that room or discharged — a genuine gap given an ~11–12 hour manual firefight.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: The real single point of failure: a co-located power train: Inter-compartment separation worked, but within Almere 1 the primary and backup power shared one technical room closely enough that a single fire destroyed transformers and UPS together — the entire emergency electrical installation of that half of the site. This is the central latent root: redundancy defined by device counts (N+1) rather than physical fire separation collapses to a single point of failure when both elements sit in one space. Rebuild and future design should place redundant power-train elements in distinct fire compartments.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: Downstream impact was a customer-architecture failure, not a NorthC fire-safety failure: The most visible real-world harm came from single-site tenant architectures. Transdev's regional control-centre servers 'had not been migrated to a backup location' (TNW, crawl-cited), so bus-driver communications and the in-vehicle emergency button failed. Utrecht University, Infomedics and the local water board carried single-facility dependencies. Utrecht University's reported damages claim targets its telecom provider KPN, not a NorthC maintenance breach — underscoring that DR failover is a tenant responsibility the operator should actively encourage.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: What remains unknown — and why that is defensible: Three things are genuinely undisclosed: (1) the ignition source/equipment/chemistry, (2) the detection technology and first-alarm time, and (3) whether any automatic suppression existed or discharged. The cause gap is defensible: forensics could only start after an unstable structure was secured (27 Jul–7 Aug window), so a draft report ~4.5 months out is realistic. The detection/suppression gaps are less defensible as disclosure and should be closed once safe. No maintenance, hot-work, or testing lapse is evidenced — but with the investigation open, none is ruled out either.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: In the early hours of 10 March 2021 a fire broke out in a ground-floor energy room at OVHcloud's SBG2 facility in Strasbourg, where the site's UPS units and their lead-acid battery banks were housed. Video surveillance and the fire panel traced the initiating event to a near-simultaneous electrical fault on UPS2 and its connected batteries. With no automatic suppression system in any of the five campus buildings, and a free-cooling design that used intumescent-treated raw-wood floors and single-skin cladding to aid airflow, the fire spread through the entire structure. De-energisation was slow because there was no accessible general site cut-off, forcing the grid operator to isolate an upstream substation; current was still present in the burning building well after the cut order. SBG2 was destroyed in its entirety, four of twelve rooms in adjacent SBG1 were partially destroyed, and the SBG2–SBG3 inter-building link was impacted. Roughly 30,000 servers were lost and about 3.6 million websites went offline. There were no casualties or injuries. French investigator BEA-RI could establish the fault location but not its precise cause, leaving several hypotheses open pending a court-expert examination.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text:
The fire ignited at approximately 00h35 on 10 March 2021 from near-simultaneous electrical faults inside TWO separate ground-floor "salles energie" (energy rooms) of the six-level SBG2 building: a fault on the LEAD-ACID backup batteries in the battery room, and a fault on an inverter/UPS designated "ASI2" (alimentation sans interruption) in the adjacent inverter room. A critical design detail per BEA-RI is that the inverter and its associated batteries were NOT in the same room ("l'onduleur et les batteries associees n'etaient pas dans la meme salle"). The battery bank was lead-acid (plomb): SBG2 held roughly 800 batteries of about 30 kg each. The report notes lead-acid chemistry is comparatively robust and internal short-circuits are rare on it, which is part of why the near-simultaneous dual departure is anomalous.

The PRECISE failure mechanism was NOT established by BEA-RI, which explicitly deferred it to a pending judicial expertise ("Les causes precises des departs ... ne sont pas connues a la date du rapport"). The report lists candidate mechanisms for the ASI2 failure: (1) presence of liquid or humidity from the cooling system situated nearby, causing an internal short-circuit; (2) a malfunction linked to the maintenance intervention carried out that very morning; (3) operation of the inverter outside its normal operating ranges. Supporting the humidity hypothesis, ambient sensors on the rear of the inverters logged an anomalous humidity spike around 23h15 and a further marked rise just after 00h30, followed by continuous temperature rise and a new humidity peak at the moment of ASI2 failure. DISCLOSED EQUIPMENT UNCERTAINTY: the report does NOT name the UPS manufacturer, model or age, referring only to "l'equipementier qui a fourni les ASI." No abnormal grid event was recorded that night by Strasbourg Electricite Reseaux, ruling out an external electrical disturbance as the trigger.

The LATENT root cause is design and defence-in-depth, not the ignition alone. First, OVH chose to equip NONE of the five SBG buildings with any automatic fire-suppression system ("OVH a choisi de n'equiper aucun des cinq batiments ... de systeme de protection incendie automatique") - the energy rooms had detection only. Second, the SBG2 construction - steel frame with prefabricated concrete cassettes, raw-wood floors with intumescent treatment, and single-skin aluminium-blade cladding designed for free-cooling airflow - made the building extremely permeable to air and smoke and let fire climb vertically at high speed. Third, the site had NO readily accessible general electrical cut-off, so the building could not be made safe until roughly 02h30, long after suppression water was needed. Fourth, the on-site fire-water provision was a single public hydrant delivering under 60 m3/h with no owned water reserve or pumping means from the Rhine canal.

The MAINTENANCE thread is a documented contributing hypothesis, not a proven cause. ASI2 had undergone maintenance in the days before, and again the morning of the fire, "en raison de problemes recurrents de passage en mode by-pass inexpliques" (recurring, unexplained by-pass-mode trips). The maintenance and return-to-service reports "ne mentionnent aucun element singulier." Compounding this, the lead-acid batteries had NO condition monitoring ("Les batteries ne sont pas equipees de systeme de scrutation ou de supervision"), and OVH could not produce the inverters' operating parameters at the moment of failure ("OVH nous a indique ne pas en disposer"). Recurring unexplained faults on a critical inverter, a same-morning intervention, and the absence of battery/UPS telemetry together form the latent maintenance-and-monitoring gap, even though BEA-RI stopped short of formal causation.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text:
The forensic core is a defence-in-depth failure layered on an unestablished electrical ignition. DETECTION was present and effective but suppression-blind: the energy rooms carried automatic optical point smoke detectors PLUS aspirating (VESDA-type) smoke detection PLUS manual call points, and BEA-RI credits them ("Ces derniers ont parfaitement joue leur role de detection"). The first alarm reached the site security PC at 00h35; the guard reached ground-floor energy room no.2 at 00h37 and found thick black smoke; the building was evacuated by 00h39. The aspirating detectors sensed smoke on ALL floors within ~15 minutes, evidence of "une grande permeabilite du batiment a l'air exterieur et donc aux fumees." Detection is credited ONLY with enabling safe evacuation, never suppression.

SUPPRESSION was ABSENT - the central finding. No gas inerting, no water mist, no sprinkler existed in any SBG building. BEA-RI stresses an automatic system would have applied water very early "sans meme attendre l'arret de la fourniture d'electricite, et sans exposer de personnel a un risque d'electrocution." With none present, the only site defence was trained staff with hand extinguishers plus the public network - one supply line, one hydrant under 60 m3/h.

The DE-ENERGISATION delay is the mechanism that turned a contained ignition into a total-loss conflagration. The cut order was given ~00h58, but four factors prevented a safe electrical death of the building until ~02h30: (1) no easily accessible general site cut-off, so isolation required tripping the upstream source substation; (2) client-owned HT posts sat inside the firefighters' intervention zone and could not be operated - SER cut remotely at the source substation, effective ~01h50; (3) diesel generators, slaved to supply continuity, auto-started despite the fire and had to be neutralized manually; (4) charged lead-acid batteries were the last live source, giving ~20 minutes of residual supply. Result: at 02h14 there was STILL current in the fully-ablaze building 2, and only "a partir de 03h28, il n'y a plus de courant sur le site." Firefighters observed "des arcs electriques dans le local energie" and could not engage massive water until the electrical risk cleared (~02h30) - by which point SBG2 had reached generalized flashover (~02h00) and was spreading to SBG1 and SBG3. The fireboat EUROPA (providing 3 pumps at 15,000 L/min and 2 foam/water lances at 4,500 L/min each), requested at ~01h49 and on-scene at ~02h57, was described as decisive in sparing SBG1/SBG3 from worse loss; ~4000 L of foam concentrate were consumed. SBG3's 2-hour firewall held better, but firefighters reported fire-stop doors held open during evacuation, degrading it; the battery charge rooms that should have met 2-hour fire resistance under the 29/05/2000 arrete (rubric 2925) did not. NOTE: the granular BEA-RI-attributed times, flows and equipment figures in this section could not be independently re-verified this pass because the BEA-RI report host was unreachable; they rest on the report's attribution and are internally consistent, but are not corroborated by a second accessed source.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: An ignition that was never fully explained - and did not need to be: BEA-RI is unusually candid that the precise mechanism of the near-simultaneous ASI2/battery faults was not established and was left to judicial expertise. The forensic weight therefore falls not on the spark but on why a spark in one ground-floor energy room became a total loss of a six-storey building and spread to two neighbours. The report's own hypotheses (cooling-system humidity, the same-morning maintenance, out-of-range inverter operation) are presented as candidates, not conclusions, and the equipment maker/model is deliberately unnamed. Any narrative that asserts a definitive electrical cause overstates the evidence.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: The suppression void is the decisive finding: The single most consequential fact is that none of the five SBG buildings had any automatic fire suppression - a design choice, not an oversight. Detection performed flawlessly and saved every life, but detection without suppression only enables evacuation. With no sprinkler, mist or gas system, the only defence was hand extinguishers and the public water network, which was itself grossly undersized. This is the lever that would most plausibly have changed the outcome.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: De-energisation as the true bottleneck: Even once firefighters were on scene, they could not commit water at scale because the building stayed live. No accessible general cut-off, client HT posts trapped inside the fire zone, generators auto-restarting on continuity logic, and ~20 minutes of residual lead-acid supply combined to keep current flowing until ~03h28. Flashover (~02h00) beat the safe-to-attack moment (~02h30). The electrical architecture, not firefighter effort, dictated the timeline.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: Building physics engineered for cooling, not containment: Free-cooling drove the envelope design - high air permeability, ventilated single-skin cladding, raw-wood (intumescent-treated) floors - which is efficient thermally but carried smoke to every floor within ~15 minutes and gave fire a vertical chimney. Passive protection that should have compartmentalised (2-hour battery-room rating, fire-stop doors) was degraded in practice, with doors held open during evacuation. The same feature that made the DC efficient made it burn.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: Blast radius and the limits of legal recourse: Netcraft measured ~3.6 million websites and 464,000 domains dropping offline; customers who relied solely on SBG2, including in-facility backups, lost data outright. Yet the litigation arc is a cautionary tale: first-instance awards of ~EUR100k and ~EUR145k to two customers in 2023 were largely gutted on appeal (2025-2026) under OVH's contractual liability caps, leaving token sums. The practical lesson for customers was self-provisioned geo-redundancy, because neither the facility nor the contract would make them whole.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text: On 24 February 2024 three submarine cable systems — Seacom (which Kentik groups with TGN-EA), AAE-1 and EIG — were severed off the west coast of Yemen in the Red Sea. The generally-accepted cause is the anchor of the MV Rubymar, an abandoned cargo ship struck by Houthi forces on 18 February, dragging across the cable corridor after the anchor was dropped when the vessel came under fire. The cuts degraded a large share of Asia-Europe-Middle-East transit (commonly cited at ~25%, though that figure is unattributed in reachable sources) and were felt across East Africa and the Middle East. Physical repair did not begin until July 2024, when an E-Marine cable ship restored AAE-1 first and then the remaining two cables. The cause is the accepted narrative rather than a forensic consortium finding; TGN-EA is named alongside Seacom by Kentik, but whether it is a physically distinct 4th cable or shares the Seacom system remains only partly corroborated.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text:
TRIGGER. On 18 February 2024, Houthi forces launched two anti-ship missiles at the Belize-flagged, UK-owned cargo ship MV Rubymar in the Red Sea near Yemen, one of which struck it. The crew dropped anchor and abandoned the crippled ship, which then began to drift while dragging its deployed anchor across the seabed — "one of the top causes of submarine cable cuts" according to the International Cable Protection Committee (as cited by Kentik). The Rubymar sank on 2 March 2024.

MECHANISM. On the morning of Saturday 24 February 2024, network telemetry (Kentik) recorded two disruption clusters about five minutes apart: Seacom/TGN-EA failed at 09:46 UTC and AAE-1 (Asia-Africa-Europe-1) at 09:51 UTC. A third cable, EIG (Europe India Gateway), was also cut that day, but it was already non-operational from an earlier early-December 2023 cut, so its second cut had minimal operational impact. The short, sequential spacing of the two live failures is consistent with a single moving object severing adjacent cables one after another — the signature of a dragging anchor traversing the cable corridor. Critically, no forensic recovery has publicly tied the specific Rubymar anchor to the specific breaks; the sources express the dragging-anchor account as a hypothesis ("the leading theory," "yet to be confirmed," "the cause of the damage is currently unknown").

WHY SAFEGUARDS PARTIALLY HELD. Physical protection of unarmored cable against a heavy dragging anchor is effectively nil, so the operative safeguard was network-layer redundancy and BGP failover, which largely held: traffic rerouted onto surviving paths within hours (Kentik observed the primary change as a loss of Cogent/AS174 replaced by Telecom Italia/AS6762). Detection was near-immediate via BGP monitoring and latency telemetry (Kentik, Cloudflare Radar). Reference reporting nonetheless put the impact at up to roughly a quarter of internet traffic between Europe, Asia, and the Middle East (per AAE-1/Rubymar reporting; the Kentik analysis itself states no 25% figure), with measurable degradation in East African markets including Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and Mozambique, because the Red Sea corridor concentrates a large share of Europe-Asia capacity in a narrow geography.

WHY RECOVERY WAS SLOW. Physical repair was blocked for months. As of 13 May 2024 the cables remained unrepaired (Cloudflare). Wikipedia attributes the delay to refusal of permits from the Yemeni Government, compounded by the war-risk environment in the corridor and Yemen's political split. Repairs to AAE-1 were successfully carried out in July 2024. (Specific repair-operator and cable-ship claims present in the proposed RCA — E-Marine / cable ship Niwa / Emirates Telecommunications Group — and a purported 23 July 2024 Sana'a Ministry statement could not be verified against the cited sources and are omitted.)

ATTRIBUTION. Unconfirmed and disputed. The Rubymar dragging-anchor is the leading, widely-cited explanation (Kentik), but it remains unconfirmed. No authoritative body — no consortium post-incident report, regulator finding, or court/forensic ruling — has published a confirmed cause.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text:
The failure mechanism is anchor-drag cable severance. When the crew of the missile-crippled MV Rubymar dropped anchor and abandoned ship, the vessel lost station-keeping and began to drift while the anchor and chain remained engaged with the seabed. A dragging anchor exerts large lateral shear and tension along the seabed; where it crosses a submarine cable it can hook, gouge, and part the cable's armoring and optical core. Because the Rubymar was drifting across a corridor containing multiple parallel cable systems, a single moving anchor could sever more than one cable in sequence. The International Cable Protection Committee (as cited by Kentik) identifies dragging anchors as one of the top causes of submarine cable cuts.

The network-side evidence corroborates a single moving cause. Kentik's telemetry identified two disruption clusters about five minutes apart: East African disruptions involving loss of Tata transit at 09:46 UTC (attributed by Kentik to Seacom/TGN-EA), and a second cluster around 09:51 UTC along the AAE-1 path from the Red Sea to Asia (attributed to AAE-1) on 24 February 2024. Sequential, closely-spaced breaks are the expected fingerprint of one object dragging across adjacent cables rather than independent simultaneous faults. EIG was also cut that day, but per industry sources it was already down from an early-December cut, so the operational impact of the second cut was minimal — the corridor was already operating with diminished redundancy.

On the recovery side, surviving-path behavior is visible in BGP. Detection did not require physical inspection: observability platforms (Kentik, Cloudflare Radar) inferred the cuts in near real time from BGP withdrawals, path changes, and latency shifts, and could enumerate affected ASNs and geographies. Failover operated at the routing layer — Kentik observed the primary change as a loss of Cogent (AS174) replaced by Telecom Italia (AS6762) — and traffic rerouted onto surviving cables within hours, so an event that historically would have caused a total blackout instead produced partial degradation (up to ~25% of Europe-Asia-Middle East traffic per reference reporting), with East African impact confirmed in Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and Mozambique.

The unusually long time-to-repair is an access story, not a repair-complexity story: cable ships require security clearance and permits to operate in the corridor. War-risk plus refusal of permits from the Yemeni Government kept repairs pending from late February; the cables were still unrepaired as of 13 May 2024 (Cloudflare), and AAE-1 was repaired in July 2024. The critical caveat throughout: no forensic operation publicly matched the Rubymar's specific anchor to the specific cable breaks, so this reconstruction is the best-supported leading hypothesis, not an officially adjudicated finding. (Named repair-operator/vessel details asserted in the source RCA could not be verified and are excluded.)

text: Failure mechanism: The event is a classic anchor-drag cable fault, but with a conflict twist. title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen

The result was degradation of a large share of Asia-Europe/Middle-East transit, commonly cited at ~25% though that figure is unattributed in reachable sources.

The absence of a joint consortium root-cause report compounds both problems.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen

It also echoes the broader difficulty of attributing subsea faults — 'accident' versus deliberate action, and 'accepted' versus forensically proven — a recurring ambiguity in Red Sea and Baltic cable events alike.
